before: One chapter having been marked off, let us also see what the other teaches us: 'Hear and give ear, and do not exalt yourselves, for the Lord has spoken. Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble on dark mountains; and you will wait for light, and there is a shadow of death, and they will be placed into darkness.' (Jeremiah 13:16)

'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult, and your eyes will bring down tears, because the Lord's flock was crushed.' He wants the same people both to hear and to give ear, not content either with their hearing alone or with their giving ear. Therefore he says: 'Hear and give ear.' Then after this he commands them not to exalt themselves, and teaches what must be done. What then is hearing and what is giving ear? Let us understand from the wording itself. 'Give ear'—receive into the ears; and 'hear'—if it is said in distinction from 'give ear'—perhaps is: receive into the mind. And among the things said in the Scriptures some are more ineffable and more mystical, and some are useful at once to those who understand. About the more ineffable I think 'hear' is said; about those useful at once and able without interpretation to benefit the hearer, 'give ear.' So if we examine the whole Scripture we will say, becoming 'approved bankers': hear this, but give ear to that.

Then when we have heard and given ear, he commands us: 'And do not exalt yourselves.' (Matthew 11:29) For 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.' (Isaiah 5:30 (cf.) And the Savior too, in saying, 'Learn from me that I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls,' (Jeremiah 13:16; Ps 23:4) teaches us not to exalt ourselves. For among the other human evils this sin also is much in us—sometimes exalting ourselves quite irrationally and over what one ought not exalt oneself even in the least, and sometimes with a semblance of reason, that what we exalt ourselves over is reasonable, yet even over that exaltation is not sound.

before: That is why Jesus baptizes (perhaps I find the meaning now) 'in the Holy Spirit and fire.' (Matthew 3:11) Not that he baptizes the same person 'in the Holy Spirit and fire,' (Hebrews 12:29) but the holy one 'in the Holy Spirit,' and the one who, after believing, after being counted worthy of the Holy Spirit, has sinned again, he washes in 'fire' — so that it is not the same person being baptized by Jesus 'in the Holy Spirit and fire.' (1 John 1:5) Blessed, then, is the one baptized in the Holy Spirit and not needing the baptism from fire. Thrice-wretched is that one who has need to be baptized with the fire. Yet Jesus has both. 'For a rod will come out of the root of Jesse, and a flower will go up from the root.' (Isaiah 11:1) A 'rod' upon those being punished; a 'flower' upon the righteous. So 'God is a consuming fire,' (Deuteronomy 4:24) and 'God is light': a consuming fire to sinners, light to the righteous and holy.

And blessed is the one who has a part in the first resurrection, who has kept the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Who is the one saved in another resurrection? The one who needs the baptism from fire, when he comes to that fire, and the fire tests him, and that fire finds wood, hay, and stubble, so as to burn them. Therefore, these things being said, gathering as far as we can the words of the Scriptures, let us store them in the heart and try to live according to them, if perhaps we may be able to become clean before the departure, and, having prepared our works for the departure, going out may be taken up in those good things and be saved in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power to the ages of the ages. Amen (1 Corinthians 3:12–13) (Luke 3:16) (Deuteronomy 4:24).

before: So that it may be said according to a simpler example able to lead you to see 'the foreskin of the heart,' I will set beside this that in the first age false opinions certainly arise in the soul. For it is not possible for a human being from the beginning to take true doctrines. The divine word foresaw history and writing according to the letter, so as to nourish the one born according to flesh to Abraham first with words according to flesh, and so that there might first be the one from the slave woman, in order that after this the one from the free woman and through the promise might be born. Why this was taken up can be understood: the foreskin of the heart comes before circumcision. So we need to take the word that cleanses the doctrines and removes everything that has come to be in us according to false opinion. This, then, is putting away the foreskin of our heart. For if the heart is, for us, what has the ruling principle—where the thoughts are, from which the reasonings go out—the one who removes evil reasonings removes 'the foreskin of the heart'; the one who puts away false opinion is circumcised as to the foreskin of his heart and becomes a man of Judah and one dwelling in Jerusalem, being circumcised.

But if someone does not put away the foreskin of his heart, let us see what the word threatens him: 'Lest my wrath go out,' it says, 'like fire and be kindled, and there will be none to quench it.' (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jer 4:4; Rom 2:29) So the wrath of the Lord goes out like fire upon those not circumcised to God, upon those who have not put away the foreskin of their heart, 'and there will be none to quench it from before the wickedness of their practices.' (Jeremiah 15:14; Lam 2:3; Ezek 22:31) That fire has as its matter the wickedness of our practices. Where there is no wickedness of practices, the fire has nowhere to spread.

That the matter of that fire is the wickedness of practices, hear the prophet saying: 'And there will be none to quench it from before the wickedness of your practices.' (Jeremiah 4:5; 6:1; Isa 58:1) 'Announce in Judah, and let it be heard in Jerusalem; say, announce, signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud.' (Jeremiah 4:5; Micah 5:2; Rev 5:5) These things announced, he says, say in Judah to those from the tribe of Judah of Christ—'for it is clear that our Savior has risen from Judah.'

before: 'And she played the harlot there. And I said after she had played the harlot in all these things: Turn to me. And she did not turn, and faithless Judah saw her faithlessness.' (Jeremiah 3:7–8)

We too have been reproached — I mean we who sin and do not keep the covenants of God, and do not see that those others, well-born, from Abraham, having received a promise, have lost the covenant. We ought then to reckon that they have fallen from the blessings and the promises, and that being from the fathers did them no good — how much more shall we, if we sin, be abandoned. 'If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham,' (John 8:39) the Savior says to them. And again John: 'Do not begin to say in yourselves, We have Abraham as father; for I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise children to Abraham' (Matthew 3:9) — hinting at us, who have a heart of stone and are hardened toward the truth. And truly God has raised children to Abraham from the stones, if we remain in the bringing-forth of children and keep the spirit of adoption.

So 'faithless Judah saw the faithlessness' (Jeremiah 3:11) of the dwelling of Israel, she who did not keep the covenants toward God, and she saw concerning all the things for which that one was left (for we, Judah, see all these things, if we read the Scripture) — that concerning the things for which the dwelling of Israel was left, in which she committed adultery, God sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce, that we might be trained by what he did to them, judging them according to the sins, abandoning them and giving them over to captivity and to slaughter and to the enemies.

We ought from these things to turn, and each of us to reckon that if God did not spare the natural branches, how much more will he not spare us. If he thrust out those from the fathers when they became sinners, what shall we who were called from the nations suffer? We have reckoned none of these things, we who were called in order that that people might be made jealous, seeing the slave honored, seeing the low-born come near. And if those suffered so many things, how much more, if we sin, shall we be abandoned?

'In the things in which the dwelling of Israel committed adultery, I sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce into her hands; and faithless Judah was not afraid' (Romans 8:15) of what I had done to the dwelling of Israel, that I sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce. She was not afraid from what had come to be for them.

Someone entered the house of a master of a house. He is newly bought. He asks whom of the former household servants the master honored and why, whom he dishonored and why. Having understood, if he wants to remain in the house of the master, he guards himself from falling into what the former slaves did who sinned and were thrown out and given over to punishment. Then, having learned what the former slaves did who were well-pleasing, and upon what sort of things they obtained freedom, he imitates those. We too were not slaves of God, but of idols and demons, Gentiles; yesterday and the day before we came to God. Let us read the Scripture, see who was justified, who was condemned; let us imitate those justified, and guard ourselves from falling into the things into which those taken captive fell, those thrown out from God (Ezekiel 11:19).

before: After this let us look at: 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained in your injustices before me, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 2:22) Did some sinning soul suppose that, taking nitre and washing with ordinary nitre, it ceases from the stain and ceases from the sin? Did someone assume that, taking this herb that springs from the earth and washing and scouring, the soul is cleansed, because the Word says here to the one who has turned into bitterness and become an alien vine, 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained in your injustices before me, says the Lord' (Hebrews 4:12)?

But one must know that the Word has all power. And as he has the power of all Scripture, so the Word has the power of every medicine, and is the power of everything that cleanses, and is most scouring. 'For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword.' (Hebrews 4:12) And whatever you name, of which there is need, that is in the power of the Word. So there is a word that is nitre, and there is a word that is soap, which, when spoken, cleanses such filth. But since not every sin is healed from such a word as is nitre, and from such a word as is soap — there are sins that do not need nitre or soap — it is said to the one who thinks it has sins of a kind that can be washed off in nitre and soap: 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained before me in your injustices, says the Lord.' (Isaiah 4:4)

And as of wounds some are healed with a poultice, and others with oil, and others need a bandage and so are made well, and there are other wounds of which it is said, 'There is no poultice to put on, nor oil nor bandages; but your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire' (Isaiah 1:7) — so there are some sins which soil the soul, and for these sins the man needs a word that is nitre, a word that is soap. And there are some sins which are not healed this way, for they are not even compared to soil. That is why the Lord in Isaiah, knowing the differences of sins, see how he says, 'The Lord will wash the soil of the sons and of the daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst with a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.' Soil and blood: soil with a spirit of judgment, blood with a spirit of burning. If you have sinned, yet not 'unto death,' you have been soiled. So 'the Lord will wash the soil of the sons and of the daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst.' (Isaiah 4:4) Then the matching: toward 'the soil,' 'with a spirit of judgment'; toward 'the blood,' 'with a spirit of burning.' And most of us, if we have sinned the worse things, do not need nitre, nor the multiplying of soap, but the spirit of burning.

before: Whether it is said to Jeremiah or to the Savior, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you' (Jeremiah 1:5): if you read Genesis and watch what is said about the making of the world, you will find that the Scripture, with a very fine distinction, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' (Genesis 1:26) For when the one according to the image was being created, 'God said, Let us make man according to our image and likeness.' He did not say, Let us form. But when he took 'dust from the earth,' he did not make the man; he 'formed the man,' and 'placed in the garden the man whom he had formed, to work it and to keep it.' (Genesis 2:15)

If you can, see the difference between making and forming. The Lord, whether to Jeremiah or to the Savior, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' (Jeremiah 1:5) For what is made does not come about in the womb; what is formed from the dust of the earth is created in the womb. 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you.' (Matthew 7:23) If the Lord knew all, he would not have said to Jeremiah as something set apart, 'I know you.' So God knows those who matter, God knows those worthy of his knowledge, and 'the Lord knew those who are his.' Those unworthy God does not know, as the Savior also does not: 'I never knew you.'

We, being men, as we advance, judge some things worthy of our knowing them. Some things we do not even want to hear, so that we may not know them. Some things we want to know. What of the God of all? Does he want to know Pharaoh? Does he want to know the Egyptians? They are not worthy of the knowledge of God. Moses is worthy, and each of the prophets of that rank. You must set many things right before God begins to know you. Jeremiah he knew before forming him in the womb. Another he begins to know at thirty years of age, another at forty. There are secret words here, not in question as regards the Savior, but as regards Jeremiah needing attention from those who have ears.

before: He has shown the complete wickedness, as having no witness of virtue at all, nor anyone who has stumbled in similar things. For what sin is like that of the one far from God and of the one who after drawing near has thrown off the reins? For “if I had not come,” (Isaiah 53:1) he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” (Lamentations 2:13) For which reason also “among those who draw near to me I will be sanctified” (John 15:22); because the one who does not know the will of the Lord and does not do it will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knows and does not do it will be beaten with many. The passion so great, then, which prophets have not been able to heal, needs God alone. before: But the words of God do not stop at 'to uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Suppose the bad things have been uprooted from me, the worse things pulled down: what good is it to me if, in place of what was uprooted, the better things are not planted? What good is it to me if, in place of these, the things that matter are not built up? That is why the words of God first, of necessity, do the 'uproot and pull down and destroy,' (1 Corinthians 1:1) and after that the 'build and plant.' And we have always watched in Scripture that the things which look grim, if I may call them so, are named first, then the things that seem cheerful are said second. 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Colossians 2:12) He did not say, 'I will make alive,' and after that, 'I will kill.' For it is impossible that what God has made alive should be taken away by him or by anyone else. But 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Hosea 6:1) Whom will I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor. 'And I will make alive,' (1 Corinthians 3:16) so that he may become 'Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ.' (2 Corinthians 6:16)

If the wretched people from the heresies had understood these things, they would not keep putting them forward to us, saying, Do you see how fierce and inhuman the God of the Law is, when he says, 'I will kill, and I will make alive'? Do you not see in the Scriptures a promise of the resurrection of the dead? Or do you not see the resurrection of the dead already making its beginning in each person? 'We were buried' with Christ 'through baptism' and we were raised with him.

So he begins from the grimmer voices, which are necessary — as 'I will kill' — then, having killed, 'and I will make alive. I will strike, and I will heal.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) 'For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives.' (Hebrews 12:6) First he strikes, and after that he heals. 'For he makes one feel pain and again restores.' (Hebrews 12:6) So also here: 'I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down and to destroy and to build and to plant.' (Job 5:18) Only, first those bad things must be taken from us. God cannot build on the place of the bad building. 'For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness?' (2 Corinthians 6:14) Vice must be uprooted from the foundations. The building of vice must be consumed from our soul, so that after these things the words of God may build and plant.

I cannot understand what is written in any other way: 'Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.' (Jeremiah 1:9) What do the words do? 'To uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' (Psalm 68:11) Words uproot 'nations'; words pull down kingdoms — not these worldly ones. Think, in a way worthy of words that pull down, worthy of words that uproot, the things uprooted by words, the things pulled down by words. Is there not, in what is being said right now, a power — if God gives it (according to 'the Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power' (1 Timothy 1:13)) — a power that uproots, if there is any unbelief, any hypocrisy, any vice, any incontinence? Amen.

before: What I mean will be clear like this: there are some who exalt themselves because they are sons of governors and because they are of a family from great worldly ranks. Such people, exalting themselves over an involuntary and indifferent matter, do not even have a plausible likelihood that what is set beside them for exaltation is reasonable. There are those who exalt themselves because they have authority to kill human beings, and who exalt themselves because they have received what among them is called such a promotion that they cut off human heads. 'The glory' of such people 'is in their shame.' Others exalt themselves over wealth—not the true wealth but the one below; and others exalt themselves, say, over having a fine house or many fields. None of these is worthy of account; one must not exalt oneself over any of these.

But the plausible case about exaltation is when someone exalts himself because he is wise, and exalts himself knowing in himself that already for ten years he has not touched sexual things, or even from childhood has not touched them; and again another exalts himself because he wore bonds concerning Christ. There is a semblance here that suggests that someone reasonably exalts himself—yet even over these, as toward the true account, no one reasonably exalts himself. So there is no reasonable exaltation even over these.

Paul had the material for exaltation through visions, through sights, through wonders and signs, through the toils he toiled for Christ, through the churches he planted, ambitious where Christ was not named to found a church. All these were material for him, if one must speak with the semblance about exaltation, that to some it would have seemed fine for him to exalt himself. But still, since even exaltation over such things is not without danger, the kind Father, as he granted him visions and sights, so also gave him in the portion of a gift 'an angel of Satan to buffet him, that he may not be exalted beyond measure.' (2 Corinthians 12:7) And about this he begged the Lord three times that the angel of Satan depart from him—the one given him that he may not exalt himself. And the Lord answered him (for Paul was worthy of the Lord's answer) and said to him: 'My grace is enough for you; for my power is perfected in weakness.' (Proverbs 18:12 (continued))

So one must exalt oneself over nothing; for falling follows exaltation according to 'Before crushing a man's heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.' So much for 'Hear and give ear, and do not exalt yourselves, for the Lord has spoken.' (Isaiah 55:2–3)

before: 'Know that I received reproach concerning you from those who set aside your words.' (Jeremiah 20:7) Let the prophet, speaking and made nothing of for what he said, be set aside by sinners; for he himself says: 'I continued being mocked.' So he was reproached by those who set aside the words spoken through him by God, and he prays, upon being reproached, to be helped by God saying: 'Know that I received reproach concerning you from those who set aside your words; finish them.' (Hebrews 11:37) Let the prophet say it, but 'finish them' spoken by the Savior fits better; for a finishing came upon Jerusalem and the people, upon what happened from the people's plot against our Savior.

After these things it is necessary—because the prophets suffered much convicting and ambassadoring the word and taking what was commanded by God—to remind the hearers about their life and their promises and our choice, so that as far as we can, if we want to have rest with the prophets, we may zealously imitate the prophets' works.

What I mean is like this: often in prayers we say: Almighty God, give our portion with the prophets, give our portion with the apostles of your Christ, that we may also be found with Christ himself. And saying these things we do not perceive what we pray; for in effect we say this: grant us to suffer what the prophets suffered, grant us also to be hated as the prophets were hated, give such words for which we will be hated, grant us to fall into as many circumstances as the apostles. For to say 'give me a portion with the prophets' (2 Corinthians 12:9–10) while neither having suffered the prophets' things nor wanting to suffer is unjust. To say 'give me a portion with the apostles' while not wanting from Paul's disposition, speaking truly, to say: 'In toils more abundantly, in blows more abundantly, in prisons beyond measure, in deaths often' and what follows, is most unjust of all. If then we want to come to be with the prophets, look at the prophets' lives—that from convicting, from rebuking, from striking they were judged, examined, condemned. 'They were stoned, they were sawn, they were tested, they died by murder of sword, they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, lacking, afflicted, mistreated, wandering upon deserts' (Hebrews 11:37–38)—when there were many synagogues of Jews; and these were 'wandering upon deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth.' What then is strange if someone wanting to zealously imitate the prophetic life, convicting, striking the one who sins, is spoken ill of, hated, plotted against? Just as also in the present such a thing had to come to be into God's church. The one who was condemned was condemned; so-and-so sitting did such things; there had to be church vindication, and it came to be; the one entrusted with the work did what he ought to have done. That one goes about speaking ill of the one who vindicated the truth. But let us not do this; let us not lend our ears to those who, because they have been cast out, speak ill of the one who cast out or of the one who became a fellow voter. The marvelous apostles, insulted countless times because of the truth, say: 'I am well pleased in weaknesses, in insults and necessities, in persecutions and distresses, for Christ.' Only may I, being insulted, know that I am insulted for no other reason than for Christ; coming into necessities, know that the ground of the necessities is Christ. May I, being abused, know that the pretext of the abuse is no other than that I vindicate the truth and ambassador for what is written, so that according to God's word everything may come to be—for this reason I am blasphemed. So let us all too, as much strength as there is, hasten upon the prophetic life, upon the apostolic life, not fleeing what is burdensome; for if an athlete flees the burdensome of the contest, he will not receive the pleasant of the crown.

before: What then? First it follows that, because of the wood, one receive the fire that consumes the wood and the grass and the straw. For our God is said—by those able to understand—to be by substance a consuming fire. And the prophet was silent about what it consumes when he said: 'Our God is a consuming fire,' but he left it for us to understand. Because he said 'God is a consuming fire,' there is something that is consumed. What then is consumed? He does not consume that which is according to the image and likeness; he does not consume his own creature, but the grass built upon it, the wood built upon it, the straw built upon it.

The place was extremely hard to narrate. There were promises, and after the promises he says: 'And I will repay first double their injustices.' (Jeremiah 5:3 or Deut 4:24) The 'first' is necessarily set beside it; for first the things of injustice are repaid, then the things of righteousness, for God does not repay in reverse. If he first repaid the goods so that we might receive the goods, and now repaid the evils, the goods would have to stop so that we might receive the evils. But first we will receive the evils, and after these the goods, so that through the disappearance of the evils the punishment of those who suffered may come to an end, and after these he may repay the goods.

Therefore you will find in the holy writings God saying first the things that seem more gloomy and after these the better: 'I will kill and make alive; I will strike, and I will heal.' (Deuteronomy 4:24) 'He himself causes pain and again restores; he struck, and his hands healed.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) Upon these things the one who understands and is piously set toward what is said can say: 'Lord, who will sojourn in your tent? Or who will encamp on your holy mountain? 'He has not taken up a reproach against those nearest him; an evildoer is despised before him, but he honors those who fear the Lord.' We will receive our sins.

before: Some said that among the exceptional ones he more clearly laments Josiah; for they were hoping through his piety for Jerusalem to be raised in the midst of nations unto glory—for Jerusalem is in the midst of nations. And this one, they say, is a type of Christ, having died through the people’s lawlessnesses. before: And since another interpretation is also necessary because of the more accurate copies having it thus: 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me,' (Jeremiah 5:3) we will interpret the saying having it this way too.

The one who indeed gives back to all their dues—fear to the one due fear, tax to the one due tax, tribute to the one due tribute, honor to the one due honor—and giving back to all what is fitting, so as not to owe what is fitting toward some, having honored parents as parents, so to speak, brothers as brothers, sons as sons, bishops as bishops, elders as elders, deacons as deacons, faithful as faithful, catechumens as catechumens—if he gives back all that is fitting, he did not owe. But if he owes doing what is fitting and has not done it, he cannot say: 'I did not owe'; for owing he did not give back. How then will I also interpret 'nor did anyone owe me'? I was lending and wanted to give the spiritual money, but they turned away from what was said and did not present themselves as receptive so as to owe; therefore no one at all owed me. For who received what was said, so that from receiving he might become a debtor of what he heard and be demanded, as a debtor of what was said, for the interest? Better then according to this for the hearer to take logical silver from the speaker and owe than, neither receiving nor taking, not even to owe.
For 'nor did anyone at all owe me' also lies among charges.

before: All the things written about God, even if they look discordant at first hearing, must be understood as worthy of the good God. Who will not say that things referred to God—that he has wrath, that he uses anger, that he regrets, even that he sleeps—look discordant? But each of these, for the one who knows how to hear dark words, will be found worthy of God.

For his wrath is not barren: as his word educates, so also his wrath educates; those not educated by word he educates by wrath. And it is necessary that God use the so-called wrath as he uses the so-named Word; for his Word is not such as everyone’s word. No one’s word is 'a living being,' no one’s word is 'God,' no one’s word was 'in the beginning' toward that one whose the Word was. So also God’s wrath is called wrath not as just anyone’s wrath. And as the Word of God has something strange beside every word of just anyone—being God, being Word as living, existing by itself, serving the Father—so once God’s so-called wrath was named, it has something strange and alien to every defined wrath.

So also his anger has something of its own; for it belongs to the purpose of the anger that refutes, wanting the one refuted to turn through the refutation. Word also refutes, as word educates; but word does not refute as anger refutes. Those not benefited by the refutation from the word will need the refutation from the anger. We said there is also a regret of God that looks discordant at first glance, since it is written: 'I have regretted that I anointed Saul as king.' (1 Samuel 15:11) Worthily seek also the regret, and do not think his regret has kinship with the regret of those who regret. As his Word had something exceptional, and his wrath something surpassing, and nothing was akin to these among the like-named, so also his regret is like-named with our regret; and like-named are those whose name alone is common, but the account of the substance according to the name is other. Therefore only the name is common of God’s anger and anyone’s anger, and only the name of anyone’s wrath and God’s wrath. So also upon regret. And the one able will seek what God’s regret works, what it worked. It took down Saul reigning lawlessly; it raised as king for the people the one according to God’s heart; for he said because of that good regret: 'I have found a man according to my heart, David son of Jesse.' (1 Samuel 13:14) But all these things are a preface for me (Jeremiah 20:7).

before: But someone will say: Even if you can refer 'he does not know' to the Savior, does it not offend you to say these things about the Only-begotten, about the firstborn of all creation, about the one announced before the conception according to the word, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you' (Luke 1:35)? And you say he does not know how to speak?

See whether you can see something worth saying, and great, about the Savior in this place: that not knowing certain things, he is greater in not knowing them than in knowing them. And I use his own voice as a witness that he does not know certain things. He says to those who tell him, 'Did we not eat in your name, and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works?' (Matthew 7:22) 'Depart from me; I never knew you.' (Matthew 7:23) Does that 'I never knew you' present his power as lesser, or as greater and more wonderful, because he did not know the worse and those who are perishing? For he knew the things that matter, the better things, and 'the Lord knew those who are his,' (John 1:1) and 'if anyone is ignorant, he is not known.' (Matthew 7:22–23) So the sinner is not known by God.

Someone among the hearers will say to me: You have shown that he does not know the sinners; you have shown that he does not know those who work lawlessness, for they are not worthy of his knowledge. How will you show that it is a great and glorious thing for the Savior to say, 'I do not know how to speak' (Hebrews 1:4)? Speaking is a human thing. To speak is to use a dialect: the speech of the Hebrews, say, or of the Greeks, or of some others. If you go up to the Savior and see him as Word 'in the beginning with God,' (John 1:1) you will see that he does not know how to speak, because speaking is human. He does not know it, because what he knows is greater than speaking. And if you compare the tongues of angels with the tongues of men, and see that he is greater even than angels, as the apostle bore witness in the letter to the Hebrews, you will say that he was greater even than the tongue of angels when he was God, the Word with the Father.

So he learns, and as it were takes on, a knowledge not of great things but of lesser and smaller ones. Just as I force myself to lisp when I talk with little children (for not knowing how to speak in baby-talk, being full-grown I force myself to talk with children), in the same way the Savior, being 'in the Father' and in the greatness of the glory of God, does not speak human things and does not know how to utter speech to those below. But when he comes into a human body he says at the beginning, 'I do not know how to speak, because I am younger.' (2 Timothy 2:19) Younger because of the bodily birth; older according to 'firstborn of all creation' (Colossians 1:15); younger because he came at the completion of the ages and visited this life later. So he says, 'I do not know how to speak' (John 14:10–11): I know things greater than speaking, I know things greater than this human sound. You want me to speak to men? I have not yet taken up a human dialect. I have your dialect, O God. I am your Word, O God. I know how to speak with you. I do not know how to speak to men. I am younger (Hebrews 9:26).

before: 'My wound is hard; from where will I be healed?' (Acts 3:21) Those who overpower me strike me, and my wound is hard. Whether he prophesies the Lord's cross (for the cross is a hard wound, as far as it lies with those who crucify him), or whether it is said about all the righteous in whom he receives a hard wound, or even if you hear this upon the prophet (for he too suffered the things written in the prophecy), it admits the same sense according to the wording that says: 'My wound is hard.' 'From where will I be healed?' Even if the Savior says: 'From where will I be healed?' he prophesies the resurrection from the dead after the hard wound; and even if it is taken upon the righteous, after the wounds healing comes again. 'Coming to be it became for me as false water, not having faith'; for the wound does not remain but passes. 'Therefore thus says the Lord: If you turn, I will also restore you.' These things are said again toward each whom God will call to turn toward him. And a mystery seems to me to be announced here in the 'I will restore you.' No one is restored into some place never having been there at all, but restoration is into what is one's own. For example if a limb of mine becomes dislocated, the physician tries to make a restoration of the dislocation.

Whenever someone comes to be outside the fatherland, whether justly or unjustly, and then receives again the power to be in the fatherland according to the laws, he was restored upon his own fatherland. Think the same with me also upon a soldier cast out from his own battle-line and being restored. So here he says toward us who turned away that, if we turn, he will restore us. For the end of the promise is also such, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles in the 'until times of restoration of all things which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old' (Acts 3:21) in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

before: 'As whom did you bear me, a man judged and examined in all the earth?' before: A prayer from Jerusalem: “See, O Lord, my dishonor,” (Genesis 25:30–34) she who has lost the adornment because of famine. And perhaps the desirable things are different—primarily the ones shown before “upon which the enemy stretched out the hand,” (Lamentations 1:11) and secondarily those of each one from the people; and the common ones he took, but in exchange for the private ones each was buying food. And toward the ascent-sense: just as Esau gave away the birthrights for the sake of red food, of which he has become namesake—Edom, that is Red earth; for he also became earthy, having despised the birthrights and having made the earthly things primary, which Jacob pursued as necessary in a secondary account because of being in a body—so also Jerusalem. But the one gives to worthy Jacob to obtain what desirable things he had, even if he did not choose these first; and the people of Jerusalem also gave for the sake of food, but not of a holy one preparing this, but of Babylonians who were going to insult the desirable things given. For Jacob knows how to adorn the things from Esau, but the Babylonians do not use the things given unto their own good. So also a soul, through lack of the necessary needs, throws away the divine lessons to those who from curiosity want to learn unto slander and mockery.

before: We are not unaware that some refer these words, as greater than Jeremiah, to our Savior and Lord. And one must know that much of it agrees with him and can be referred to the Savior — I will set that out. But a few of the things said to Jeremiah press the argument, and cannot, as most people take them, be fitted to the Savior.

What then fits the Savior? 'To all to whom I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 1:7–8) These would not yet clearly seem to be referred to the Savior. But what follows puts the reading about Jeremiah in a tight place: 'And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me, Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down.' (Jeremiah 1:9–10) What nations did Jeremiah uproot? What kingdoms did he overthrow? For it is written, 'Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down.' (Jeremiah 1:6) And what authority did Jeremiah have 'to destroy'? And whom did he build in such numbers that it should be said 'and to build'? Jeremiah says, 'I have not profited, and no one has profited me.' (Colossians 2:9) How then is 'to build and to plant' given to him? How will 'to plant' fit Jeremiah?

These things, referred to the Savior, do not press the interpreter, because in them Jeremiah is a symbol of the Savior. But what I am about to set down presses even the most intelligent person who wants to show how these too can fit the Savior: 'And I said, You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak.' (Jeremiah 15:10) He who is Wisdom, he who is the Power of God, who brought us 'the fullness of the deity, which dwelt in him bodily' (1 Corinthians 1:24) — how then can 'I do not know how to speak' fit the Savior? And 'I am younger' is forbidden to the Savior, as if he were saying it wrongly. For if the Lord says to him, Do not say this, it is clear that he forbids what is not well said. So these do not fit the Savior. Those other words do not seem to put the Savior to shame.

To say that these belong to Jeremiah and those to the Savior is not hard. But a fair-minded person will be much pressed here. To cut a connected run of words, and to say, 'These, being lesser, fit Jeremiah and not Christ, and these, being greater than Jeremiah, fit Christ and not Jeremiah' — that is the work of people without judgment. Let the whole, then, be referred to Jeremiah, and let even the things that seem greater than Jeremiah be interpreted.

before: After these things let us look at what concerns the belt. For 'thus says the Lord: Go and get yourself a linen belt, and put it around your waist, and you shall not pass it through water.' (Jeremiah 13:1) And I got a belt according to the word of the Lord and put it around my waist. And the word of the Lord came to me saying: 'Take the belt that is around your waist, and rise and go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in the cleft of the rock.' (Jeremiah 13:11) After days he goes there and finds this belt rotten. And the Lord adds, giving the occasion for interpreting the belt, saying: 'As the belt is glued to a man's waist, so I glued to myself the house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, says the Lord, to become for me a people named and a boast and a glory—and they did not listen to me.' So the prophet is taken in God's place, girding the linen belt around his waist, as God girded the people: 'For I glued this people to myself,' he says—as if the people becomes God's belt.

But why does it become God's belt around his waist? Let the one able, reading Ezekiel and seeing God as it were embodied by the word—and how what is from the waist downward is fire, and what is from the waist is electrum—search out the word, why what is below God is fire. The matters from the waist and from generation—these are fire. For everything in generation needs the cleansing that comes from fire; everything in generation needs chastisement. But what is above the waist and has gone beyond generation—these are matter as in what is purest and most precious; for electrum is said to be more valuable than gold.

Since then Scripture uses examples in order to teach that God's body above is more honorable and the body below is lesser, for this reason it introduced God composed of fire and electrum. And each of us in generation is fire; we are not the electrum. But if we ascend and make progress—for it is possible to move from being today among the things below, so as to become God's body above—we will be, having crossed the fire, the electrum around God's higher body. So he glues around his waist the linen belt.

To what end? That it may be shown that the people is as it were a covering of God. For against those who want to accuse God the people stands and as it were shields him and does not allow anything out of place to be said about God. But when we sin, just as the prophet puts this belt away and condemns it to the Euphrates river so that it may be destroyed there, so the one who sins is cast away from God's waist, and having been cast out is thrown into the Euphrates river—the river of Mesopotamia, where the Assyrians are enemies to Israel, where the Babylonians are—and there he is destroyed. For though there are so many rivers, the prophet is sent from Judea to the Euphrates river to deal with and lead away a linen belt.

And why also 'linen'? Because it has its origin from earth; for it is a plant rising from earth, then after being cultivated it is carded and washed and scrubbed and made with much working, so that it may become such as to be a belt or whatever else. We too then all have our origin as God's belt, and having our origin from earth we need much preparation, that we may be carded, that we may be washed, that we may put away the color of the earth. For the color of linen's origin is one thing, and that from the working another. The color of linen's origin is rather black, but from the working it becomes most bright. Something of this kind also reaches us who are in generation. We are black according to the beginning in believing; therefore at the beginning of the Song of Songs it is said: 'I am black and beautiful.' And we at the start resemble Ethiopians in the soul. Then we are scrubbed clean, that we may become brighter according to 'Who is this who comes up whitened?' And we become 'bright and clean linen,' then also we are woven onto God's belt when we are worthy to be glued to God. God does not put us away. He put away the first people—'the whole house of Judah' and 'the house of Israel.'

It came to be so as not to be used any longer; for he no longer girds them around himself. In their place God has girded us; for having cast off the belt he did not remain naked, but wove another belt for himself. This belt is the church from the nations—which should know that 'if God did not spare the former, how much more will he not spare her either if she sins,' (Romans 11:21) unless she is worthy of God's waist. 'But the one glued to the Lord is one spirit' in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever. Amen.

before: And this too must be added to the argument: if it was Samuel, and when he went out the Holy Spirit stood away from him, and prophecy stood away from him, then the apostle who says is not true: “Now I prophesy in part, and I know in part; but when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be abolished.” (1 Corinthians 13:9–10) Therefore the perfect is after this life. And if Isaiah prophesied anything, he prophesied in part with all boldness; and David has been witnessed here unto the perfect of prophecy. Therefore Samuel did not cast away the prophetic grace.

And that he did not cast it away—he used it thus, as those who speak in tongues, so that one might say: “My spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (1 Corinthians 14:14)? And yet the one who speaks in a tongue does not build the church; for Paul says that the one who prophesies builds the church, saying in those very words: “But the one who prophesies builds a church.” (1 Corinthians 14:4) But if “the one who prophesies builds a church,” (Psalm 51:11) and he had prophetic grace—for he had not lost it, not having sinned; for only the one loses prophetic grace who after prophesying has done things unworthy of the Holy Spirit, so that it leaves him and flees from his ruling part—which David also feared then after the sin, and said, “And do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Genesis 3:24)—if therefore the Holy Spirit prophesies, and Samuel was a prophet, and “the one who prophesies builds a church,” (Luke 16:23–24) whom does he build? Does he prophesy into heaven? To whom—to angels, who have no need? “It is not those who have need, but those who are badly off.” (John 14:6) Some need his prophecy; for prophetic grace is not idle, and none of the gifts in the Holy One is idle. Therefore of the prophetic grace the souls of those who sleep (if I may also say so) had need. But here Israel had need of the prophet; and the one who sleeps, released from life, also had need of the prophets, so that again the prophets might proclaim Christ’s sojourn to him.

Besides, before my Lord Jesus Christ’s sojourn it was impossible for anyone to pass through where the tree of life is; impossible to pass the things appointed to guard the way of the tree of life: “He placed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns to guard the way of the tree of life.” (John 10:7–9) Who could make a way? Who could make anyone pass the flaming sword? Just as no one could make a way through the sea except the one of the fiery pillar, the pillar of light from God; just as no one could make a way through the Jordan except Jesus— of whom that Jesus was a type of the true God—so through the flaming sword Samuel could not pass, nor Abraham. For this reason Abraham also is seen by the one being punished, and the rich man, being in torments, lifting his eyes sees—even if from afar, yet he sees—and Lazarus in the bosom. Therefore patriarchs and prophets and all were waiting for my Lord Jesus Christ’s sojourn, so that he might open the way. “I am the way; I am the door.”

There is a way to the tree of life, so that you may become one who passes through fire—“a flame will not burn you”: of what fire? “He placed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns to guard the way of the tree of life.” (Isaiah 43:2) So for this reason those blessed ones were waiting there, doing an economy and unable to be where the tree of life is, where God’s paradise is, where God is farmer, where the blessed and elect and holy ones of God come to be.

before: It is said to those who have sinned: 'Sow wheat and reap thorns.' (1 Corinthians 4:1 ('Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God')) For even if they deal with the oracles of God, those who do not deal with them well, nor live as they ought, nor believe, sow wheat and reap thorns. Especially this can be understood of the heterodox who meet the Scriptures and reap thorns not from the Scriptures but from their own inventions. 'Their lots will not benefit them.' (Luke 12:42 ('And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward...')) Others have also explained these things. And since we do not reject their explanation, we fairly bring it into the open—not as ourselves discovering it but as having learned a good lesson. This word will benefit both you and us if we pay attention to what is written—we who seem to be of a certain lot, seated in front of you, so that some want to come into this lot.
But know that the lot does not save in every case. For many elders too will perish, and many of the laity will be shown blessed.

Since then there are some in the lot who do not live so as to be benefited and to adorn the lot, therefore, say those who explained it, it is written: 'Their lots will not benefit them.' For what benefits is not the mere sitting in the eldership, but living worthily of the place, as the word requires. The word requires you also to live well, and us. But if one may put it so—'the mighty will be examined mightily' (Jeremiah 4:3 or Hos 10:12 (cf. 'break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns'))—more is required of me than of the deacon, more of the deacon than of the layperson, and the one entrusted with the rule of us all, the church's rule itself, is required still more. Therefore the apostle who was entrusted with great things says—listen—'Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.' (Jeremiah 5:3 (LXX) or Mic 3:11 ('they lean upon the Lord, saying...') — but closer to Jer 5:3 context of ineffective rites)
Here then seek among the stewards that someone faithful be found. And so rare it is to find a steward faithful and good.

So much for 'Their lots will not benefit them.'

before: God condemned Jerusalem for her sins, and they had been judged to be left to captivity. Even so the God who loves mankind, when the time had come, sends this prophet also, starting two reigns before the captivity, so that those who were willing, taking it in, might repent through the prophetic words. He sent a prophet to prophesy under the second king after the first, and under the third, up to the very times of the captivity.

For the long-suffering God was giving a delay even, so to speak, one day before the captivity, urging those who heard to repent, so that the grim things of the captivity might cease. That is why it is written that Jeremiah prophesied 'until the captivity of Jerusalem, until the fifth month.' (Jeremiah 1:3) He had begun, and he was still prophesying, as if to say: you have become captives; even so, repent. If you repent, the captivity will not go on, but the mercy of God will stand over you.

So we have something useful from the record that gives the times of the prophecy: that God, according to his own love of mankind, urges those who hear not to suffer the things of the captivity. It is like this with us too. If we sin, we also are about to become captives. For 'to hand such a one over to Satan' (1 Timothy 1:20) differs in nothing from handing those from Jerusalem over to Nebuchadnezzar. before: Let these things be said by me as in a digression upon 'Woe is me, mother.' But upon us let him not say 'Woe is me,' and upon us let the angels of the heavens not say it. When our Savior says 'Woe is me,' they too will say 'Woe is me'; for they are not better than our Savior, and they also see our stumbles. But blessed are those over whom the angels will not say 'Woe is me,' but rather bless them: for 'there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents rather than over ninety-nine who have no need of repentance.' These things for comfort.

before: Let us also look at the necessary rebuke next, which it is good to take up in the ethical place, saying: 'Be ashamed of your boasting, of reproach before the Lord.' (Jeremiah 9:23–24) There are things in which we boast through folly, though they are not worthy of boasting. For example, if someone boasts that he is rich and possesses much, one might say to him: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.'

If someone boasts of this outward nobility, it will be said to him: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.' If someone boasts of costly clothing, of a house built richly, that boasting is foreign to the boasting of the saints; therefore it will be said to such a one: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.' Hear the word of the prophet Jeremiah commanding us not to boast even in wisdom: 'Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom,' (Jeremiah 9:23) he says, 'nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his wealth, but let the one who boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am the Lord.' Hear what kinds of boasts he boasts: 'In labors more abundantly'—which of us can say this?—'in prisons beyond measure, in deaths often.'

before: 'Signal with a trumpet upon the earth.' (Numbers 10:2–3) The lofty word—the one that wakes the hearer, that prepares him for the fight against the passions and against the activities of opposing powers, that prepares him for the heavenly festivals (for it is said with a view to both)—is taken as a trumpet.

In Numbers such a word is a trumpet. For example, the word commands me—and anyone else to whom it is given who wills and has sought the mind of the Scriptures—to make 'silver trumpets, hammered work.' So the word says: 'Signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud; say: Gather yourselves and let us enter the walled cities.' (Jeremiah 4:7) The word of God does not want us to enter an unwalled city, but into the church of the living God, walled by the strength of the Word—for he is the wall. In the seventeenth Psalm it also lies that God is a wall. 'Taking it up, flee into Zion.' As many of you as are outside Zion, 'taking it up, flee into Zion; hurry, do not stand still.' (Psalm 9:11 (LXX)) You who are in progress, hurry to the Lookout, 'for I am bringing evils from the north and a great crushing' (Psalm 139:12 (LXX))—evils brought 'from the north'—from the opposing one, the north, as has often been said. Whoever is found not hurrying and not entering 'into the walled cities,' not becoming 'in the churches of God,' but standing outside, will himself be caught by the enemies and destroyed. Who is the enemy? Let us see from what follows how it is said: 'A lion has gone up from his den; destroying nations he has carried them off.' This is the enemy we must flee. A lion pursues us. Who is this? Peter teaches, saying: 'Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may swallow (1 Peter 5:8); resist him, firm in the faith.' And according to the ninth Psalm he 'lies in wait in secret; he lies in wait like a lion in his den.' And this lion does not lie in wait by day, but when night has come. For according to the hundred-and-third Psalm: 'You set darkness, and it became night. In it all the beasts of the wood will pass through, young lions roaring to snatch and to seek from God food for themselves.'

before: 'If he removes his abominations from his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears: “As the Lord lives,” (Jeremiah 4:1–2) in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.'

Let us look at ourselves who swear—how we do not swear in judgment but without judgment, so that our oaths come by habit rather than by judgment. We are carried away, and the word, exposing this, says: 'And if he swears, “As the Lord lives,” (Jeremiah 4:2) in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.' We know what the Lord said to the disciples in the Gospel: 'But I say to you, do not swear at all.' Let us look at this saying too; and if God grants, both will be examined together. Perhaps one must first swear 'in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.'

In the one who swears I first look for what is not false but true, so that he may swear with truth. Yet we wretched ones even swear falsely. But even if it is 'with truth,' an oath is still not well made unless it is also 'in judgment.' For grant that I swear by habit—I do not swear 'in judgment.' If one must take for such an oath the God of all and his Christ upon this matter, how great must the matter be before I bend the knee and swear? Perhaps I would do it sometime to heal unbelief that has arisen in some about my word.
He has joined both—those from the nations and Israel. He spoke about the nations; he spoke also about Israel (Matthew 5:34) (John 10:16 or Eph 2:14–16).

before: There is therefore no stumbling-block in the passage, but all things have been written wondrously and have been understood by those to whom God may reveal them. And we who have come upon the completion of the ages have something extra. What extra? If we are released from here, becoming good and excellent, not bringing on ourselves the burdens of sin, we too will pass through the flaming sword and will not go down into the country where those who slept before his presence were waiting for Christ; but we will pass through, harmed in nothing by the flaming sword.

And each one’s work—of what sort it is—the fire itself will test. If someone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved thus, as through fire. We will therefore pass through; and we have something more, and we cannot, having lived well, depart badly. before: For we seek whether, as everyone’s anger is evil but God’s is refuting, and everyone’s wrath is harsh but God’s so-called wrath is educative, and our regret accuses weakness in the one before the regret, but upon God his regret does not accuse God but the outward affairs upon which the regret is taken—so also one must understand the deception of God as of another kind beside our deception with which we deceive. What then is the deception beside God’s, which the prophet understood when he ceased being deceived, and says, knowing the benefit from having been deceived: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived' (Jeremiah 20:7)?

And first I will use a Hebrew tradition that has come to us through someone who fled because of the faith of Christ and because of having gone up from the law and having come where we spend time. He told either a story that appears or a word able to lead the hearers to 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived.' (Jeremiah 20:7) He said such things: God does not tyrannize but reigns, and reigning he does not force but persuades, and wants those under him to offer themselves willingly to his economy, that someone’s good may not be according to necessity but according to the willing. Which Paul also knowing said in the letter to Philemon about Onesimus: 'that your good may not be according to necessity but according to willing.' (Philemon 1:14) The God of all could then make a supposed good in us, that of necessity we give alms and of necessity be temperate, but he has not wished it. Therefore he does not command us to do what we do from grief or from necessity, that what comes to be may be willing. He seeks a way, so to speak, how someone may willingly do what God wants.

The tradition then also told me something such: he wanted to send Jeremiah to prophesy to all the nations and before all the nations to the people. But since the prophecies had something more gloomy—for they announced punishments which each according to worth will be punished—and he knew the prophet’s choice not wanting to prophesy the worse things to the people of Israel, for this reason he managed to say: 'Take this cup, and you will make all the nations drink to whom I will send you.' before: What the prophet is commanded by God to say ought to be worthy of God. Yet if we remain on the letter it does not appear worthy of God, so that someone hearing the letter might say: these letters are folly. But a psychic person will say this; for 'the psychic person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are folly to him.' (1 Corinthians 2:14)

Look then at what the wording says. 'And you shall say to this people: Thus says the Lord the God of Israel'—what 'the Lord the God of Israel' says, let it be worthy of the Lord of Israel—'Every wineskin will be filled with wine. And if they say to you, “Shall we not know, knowing, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?” (Deuteronomy 32:32)' And those who answer, if they say these things standing on the bare wording, claim to know that 'every wineskin will be filled with wine,' and they lie. For not every wineskin will be filled with wine. There are wineskins filled with oil or with some other liquid substance. So some lie; for not every wineskin will be filled with wine. And the people answers saying: 'Shall we not know, knowing, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?'—words that will receive an interpretation of this kind, as far as we can.

If we know the differences among wines and what is said about them, and accordingly look at the wineskins, we will see that it is true that every wineskin will be filled with wine. For whether someone is good—let us name him so among wineskins, a wineskin—he will be filled with wine according to his own goodness. Or whether he is, by comparison of wineskins and the judgment about them, wicked, he too according to his wickedness will be filled with wicked wine. How then can we take from Scripture the different wines? About the worse ones it is written like this: 'For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot from Gomorrah.

Their grape is a grape of gall; a cluster of bitterness to them; their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps.' And about the better ones: 'Your cup that makes drunk is as the strongest,' (Psalm 78:47 or Isa 28:2) and Wisdom calls to her own mixing-bowl saying: 'Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you.' (Psalm 23:5 (LXX)) So there is wine from Sodom, and there is wine that Wisdom mixes. And again: 'A vineyard came to be for the beloved on a horn in a rich place,' planted by God, the vine called Sorek—choice and marvelous. And there is also a vine of the Egyptians, which God strikes according to what is written: that 'God struck their vine with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.'

before: And to either interpretation of Jerusalem the next words also fit: 'You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You will go backward.' (Matthew 24:18) That you have turned away from the Son of God, and through turning away from the Son of God have turned away from God—what need is there even to say it? And since the Jerusalem in Judea turned away from the Christ—from which all the Jews are to be understood—therefore 'You will go backward.' For there was a time when she did not go backward but forward; but now she goes backward, 'and they turned in their hearts toward Egypt' (Luke 17:32)—clearly so that they might go backward. Concerning what 'You will go backward' is, or what it is to stretch forward to the things ahead, we will set it out like this.

The righteous stretches forward to the things ahead, forgetting the things behind. Clearly the one disposed contrary to the righteous remembers the things behind and does not stretch forward to the things ahead. Remembering the things behind, he disobeys Jesus teaching and saying, 'Let him not turn back to take his cloak' (Luke 9:62); he disobeys Jesus saying, 'Remember Lot's wife'; he disobeys Jesus saying, 'No one who puts hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of God.' (Genesis 19:17) And in the law it is written that the angels said to Lot who had gone out from Sodom: 'Do not look back, and do not stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' And this also has a sense worthy of an angelic spirit: 'Do not look back'—always stretch forward to the things ahead. You have left Sodom; do not turn toward Sodom. You have left wickedness and sin; do not turn back to it, 'and do not stand in all the surrounding country.' Even if you keep the former command that says, 'Do not look back,' it is not enough for you to be saved unless you also hear the second command that says, 'And do not stand in all the surrounding country.' For one who has begun to progress must not stand in the country around Sodom, even if he has crossed Sodom, but having crossed from standing in the surrounding country he must be saved onto the mountain, according to 'Do not look back and do not stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' If you want not to be taken along with the people of Sodom, never turn back, and do not stand in the country around Sodom, and be nowhere else than on the mountain—for only there is it possible to be saved.
And the mountain is the Lord Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever. Amen.

before: I want to see what follows. It can be referred both to the prophet, according to one narrative, and to the Savior. Let us look also at what comes next: 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me.' Even if we have read it this way, we must also know that most copies of the Seventy’s edition do not have it so; later, when we examined the remaining editions as well, we learned that it is a scribal error. before: But I said these things beforehand, before I interpret 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me.' (Jeremiah 2:36 or similar lament) For the writing is double: in most copies 'I did not benefit, nor did anyone benefit me,' (Job 22:3 or Jeremiah 2:36 (LXX)) but in the most accurate and those agreeing with the Hebrew 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me.' So one must both interpret what is commonly current and carried in the churches and not leave unexplained what is from the Hebrew writings. He then proclaimed the word; no one received what was said. As a physician also used up the medicines, the sick being undisciplined and filling their own desires.

Perhaps there is a reciprocal affection through the love of humanity of the one benefited toward the one who benefited, so that the speaker also comes to be benefited, since blessed is the one who speaks into ears that hear.

before: Who is the one saying, 'Through me the whole land was made desolate with desolation' (Matthew 23:32)? Christ says these things. Before his sojourn many sins had indeed come to the people, but not of such a kind that they should be abandoned altogether and handed over to a long captivity. before: 'Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains.' (Jeremiah 13:16) There are dark mountains; there are bright mountains. Bright mountains are the holy angels of God, the prophets, Moses the servant, the apostles of Jesus Christ. All these are bright mountains, and about these I think it has been said in the Psalms: 'His foundations are in the holy mountains.' (Matthew 17:20) And what are dark mountains? Those who lift up heights against the knowledge of God.

The devil is a dark mountain; the rulers of this age who are being abolished are dark mountains; and the demon of epilepsy was a mountain, and it was a dark mountain, about which the Savior said: 'You will say to this mountain.' For when the account of epilepsy was being sought and the disciples said, 'Why could we not cast it out?' the Savior answers that 'If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain' (Matthew 17:20)—about which you put forward the question, about which you sought—'You will say to this: Move from here to there, and it will move.' (Psalm 23:4) 'From here' from the human being, 'there' to its own place. So those who stumble do not stumble on bright mountains but on dark mountains, when they come to be with the devil and his angels, the dark mountains. 'And you will wait for light.' Yet it can also be joined to 'Give glory to the Lord our God'—the 'and you will wait for light.'

If you give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains, clearly even if it grows dark you will wait for the light and the light will succeed you. But another might say (I do not know whether understanding soundly or not) that even those who stumble 'on dark mountains' will wait among the dark mountains waiting for the light of mercy; for this will seem to be the 'and you will wait for light.' And when someone comes upon the dark mountains, let us see what is there: 'shadow of death.'

Where the dark mountains are, there is a shadow of death generated from the dark mountains themselves. 'And they will be placed into darkness.' 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' Of those who hear, some hear in a hidden way, and some, even if they hear, do not hear in a hidden way. What then is hearing in a hidden way but 'But we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predetermined before the ages for our glory' (1 Corinthians 2:7)? And again elsewhere it is said that 'most of God's works are in hidden things.' If I hear the law, I either hear in a hidden way or I do not hear in a hidden way.

The Jew does not hear the law in a hidden way; therefore he is circumcised openly, not knowing that it is not 'the one who is a Jew openly, nor the circumcision openly in flesh.' But the one who hears circumcision in a hidden way will be circumcised in secret; the one who hears the things legislated about the Passover in a hidden way eats from the sheep of Christ—for 'our Passover was sacrificed, Christ'—and knowing what the flesh of the Word is like, and knowing that 'it is true food,' he partakes of it; for he heard the Passover in a hidden way. But this common Jew for this reason killed the Lord Jesus and is still today liable for Jesus' murder, since he heard neither the law nor the prophets in a hidden way.

If you read about the unleavened breads, one can hear the command in a hidden way, and one can hear it openly. As many of you as (for the Passover is near) keep unleavened breads, the bodily unleavened breads, you do not hear the command that says: 'If you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep.' And about the Sabbath women who have not heard the prophet do not hear in a hidden way but hear openly. They do not bathe on the Sabbath day; they return 'to the poor and weak elements,' as if Christ had not sojourned—the one who perfects us and carries us across from the legal elements to the Gospel perfection.

For this reason let us attend, reading the law and the prophets, lest we fall under the prophecy that says: 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' As many as keep the Jewish fast as not understanding the day of atonement after Jesus Christ's sojourn—you did not hear the atonement in a hidden way, but only openly; for to hear the atonement in a hidden way is to hear how God set Jesus as atonement for our sins, and that 'he is atonement for our sins, not for ours only but also for the whole world.' And even if Gospel parables are read and the hearer is one of those outside, he will not hear them in a hidden way.

But if the hearer is an apostle or one of those entering 'into Jesus' house,' he comes to Jesus, inquires also about the unclearness of the parable, and Jesus interprets it, and that hearer of the Gospel becomes one hearing it in a hidden way, so that his soul may not weep; for the soul of those not hearing in a hidden way weeps.

How marvelously he did not say: you will weep, if you do not hear in a hidden way, but: 'your soul will weep.' There is a weeping of the soul alone weeping, and perhaps the Savior teaches us that weeping when he says: 'There will be the weeping.' And even if he says: 'Woe to those who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep,' he speaks about that weeping which the prophet also threatens here saying: 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' For when you are insulted, then you will weep and your eyes will bring down tears, because the Lord's flock was crushed. If someone now sees the Jewish things and compares them with the ancient, he will see in what way the Lord's flock was crushed.

For this was once the Lord's flock, and since they judged themselves unworthy, the word turned to the nations. If then that flock of the Lord was crushed, we the wild olive, grafted contrary to its nature into the cultivated olive of the fathers—ought we not fear more, lest this 'flock of the Lord' also be crushed? For it is going to be crushed sometime according to what was said by the Savior, when 'because lawlessness is multiplied the love of many will grow cold.' About whom is the word? Is 'the love of many will grow cold' not said about those called Christians? About whom is the word, that 'When the Son of Man comes, will he find the faith on the earth?' (Luke 18:8) Is it not about us? For this reason let us attend to ourselves, doing everything, that day by day this flock of God may be improved, healed, cured, and every crushing depart from our souls, that we may be perfected in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever.
Amen.

before: She said the cause of the lamentations to be that there is none turning her soul back—or, according to Symmachus, reclaiming it. And she says the sons also have vanished, the enemy having been empowered through the things in which they were sinning; for when we are pious he does not prevail—for he is weak when we advance, and is put to death when we are perfected, and is crushed under the feet, being made fine as dust before the face of wind, and as mud of streets being made fine. For analogously to the things in which we sin he is fed and gains power; but when we have ceased from stumbling he is as it were destroyed by famine. And from the opposites: when we do well we strengthen the divine powers for ourselves, and when we sin we chase them away. For which reason Symmachus instead of “vanished” (Lamentations 1:16) rendered “deserted.” (Psalm 18:42) And a contemplative soul would say these things—being of the Word of the truth and through slackness having lost this gladdening Word and all the fruits that are named her sons—because wickedness hostile against her has been empowered (Romans 16:20).

before: 'Let each turn from his evil way, and make your practices better.' (Jeremiah 5:3) Sometimes the more simple say: Blessed are the older humans, because they heard the Lord through the prophet saying: 'And the Lord spoke to them.' And now the Lord says also to us through the things written: 'Let each turn from his evil way'; the Lord himself converses with you saying: 'And make your practices better.'

But these answered to whom the exhortative words about repentance were spoken, and let us see what they answered, that we too may not answer such things. What then answering do they say? 'We will take courage, that we will go behind our turnings-away, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart.' (Jeremiah 2:30 or Jer 31:22) And if you do not say it in words, but your life is such as to sin, you also say by force through the evil deeds after the exhortative words: 'We will take courage…'

And what is 'we will go behind our turnings-away'? Those who began to put the hand to the plow and those being taught turned away from the base things. Whenever then someone putting the hand to the plow turns to the things behind, he will go 'behind his turnings-away'; for he will go behind those things from which he turned away, and he runs back upon those sins which he left. And of those hearing these things, whether catechumens who left the gentile life or faithful already advanced in stretching forward to the things ahead, if the life has become wretched, they say nothing other than: 'We will go behind our turnings-away, and each will do the pleasing things of his evil heart.' For there is an evil heart and there is a good heart. Therefore let no one go 'behind his turnings-away' nor do 'the pleasing things of his evil heart.'

'Therefore,' toward those answering these things, 'says the Lord: Ask now among the nations: Who has heard such fearful things which virgin Israel has done exceedingly?' If the church from the nations asks among the nations, it will be said: Hear what fearful things virgin Israel has done. For let us compare the life of those who sinned with the life of those who turned and believed, and we will know that those did fearful things, killing 'the Lord of glory,' but these turned to him who was killed and died by those for the sins of the world.

before: 'Because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord. And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me, and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me.' Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot.' (Jeremiah 1:5)

There is one kingdom, the general sin of greed and of robbery, and there are many kingdoms in those who have many kinds of sins. Then, in each of the sinners, think of the nations under the kingdom: this man has many nations of the kingdom according to fornication, that man has many nations of the kingdom according to robbery, according to slander, according to anger.

before: Those who pronounce the prophets blessed, and in blessing them pray to have their share with the prophets, gather from the prophetic words the choice things of their prophecy. They seek to be persuaded that if they live according to those things—even if something harsh meets them in this life when they imitate the prophetic life—they will obtain rest and blessedness with the prophets.

From many places one can gather the prophets’ excellences: their freedom, their taut energy, their watchfulness, their being aroused—that when circumstances came they did not worry, because of that freedom, only that they might rebuke, only that they might turn people back, as prophets do when they speak the word of God with boldness, striking those who sin, even if those being rebuked seemed able to do great things.

But even if one can do this from everywhere, let us see it also from what was read today. The prophet rebuked many, and the prophet spoke to many; for he lived among people who had become sinners, as is clear from the captivity that took place in his times. Having rebuked many, and having been judged by many, he utters such words as these (Jeremiah 52:4–11) (Jeremiah 7:25–26).

before: 'A lion has gone up from his den.' (Jonah 3:5–8 or Joel 1:13–14 (sackcloth and lament)) Where? When? He is down, having fallen; he has come down into the lowest parts of the earth. So he comes 'to make your land' desolate, so that the lion may trample the seeds, so that he may make your land empty. 'And your cities will be torn down because they are not inhabited.' (Isaiah 5:6 or 7:23–25 (trampling of vineyard) Upon these things, gird yourselves with sackcloth.

before: Jeremiah prophesied, and Pashhur son of Immer the priest heard the words of the prophecy.
