And it is written that hearing the words of this prophecy Pashhur struck Jeremiah, and was not content with having struck him, but also threw him into a certain fall-pit. Scripture cared to say also where this fall-pit was—in the gate of Benjamin—and that the fall-pit was in a place where there was an upper room, and an upper room of no other than the house of the Lord. These things the Holy Spirit wrote as having come to be upon the prophecy to Jeremiah, and as having come from Pashhur.

Then it says: on the next day Pashhur led Jeremiah out of the fall-pit. No longer do the works of the flesh spring up in the righteous, with which the flesh used to flourish—no longer fornication, no longer uncleanness, no longer sensuality, no idolatry, no sorcery, and the rest. And the Savior also says: 'Do you think that I came to cast peace upon the earth? I did not come to cast peace but a sword.' (Matthew 10:34) Truly, before he came there was no sword upon the earth, nor did 'the flesh desire against the Spirit, nor the Spirit against the flesh.' But when he came and we were taught what belongs to the flesh and what to the Spirit, the teaching, become like a sword on earth, divided the flesh and the earth from the Spirit. And 'the earth was made desolate' when we carry about the putting-to-death of Jesus in the body, and we no longer live according to flesh, but the Spirit lives, and we sow nothing into the flesh but everything into the Spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh but from the Spirit eternal life.

before: 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations.' (Jeremiah 1:5) If you look for this in Jeremiah — 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations' (Deuteronomy 18:15) — watch later on: he is commanded to prophesy 'against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 48:1) and there is a heading, 'What Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations,' (Deuteronomy 18:19) against Elam, against Damascus, against Moab. And we have it that he 'prophesied against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 25:13) as regards the letter of 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations,' (Jeremiah 49:34) said to him.

If it is a matter of the higher sense: if of Jeremiah, we have already spoken; if of the Savior, what need is there even to say it? He truly prophesied to all the nations. For he is, as he is ten thousand other things, also a prophet. As he is high priest, as he is savior, as he is physician, so he is also prophet. Moses, prophesying about him, did not say only 'a prophet,' but said it with a special force: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your brothers, like me (Deuteronomy 18:15); him you shall hear, and it shall be that whoever does not hear that prophet shall be destroyed from his people.' (Jeremiah 49:23)

This one, then, is also the prophet set 'to the nations,' and he received grace from God poured out on his lips, so that not only when he was present in the body, but also now, when he is present in power and in the Spirit, he may prophesy 'to all the nations,' so that from all the nations his prophecy may reach its end and draw men to salvation (Acts 3:22–23) (Psalm 45:2).

before: 'And faithless Judah was not afraid, and she went and played the harlot also.' (Jeremiah 3:8–10) Israel having played the harlot first, Judah later played the harlot too. 'And her harlotry came to nothing, and she committed adultery with the wood and the stone.' (Romans 11:25–26) When we sin, we do nothing else than, becoming stone-hearted, commit adultery with the stone. When we sin and play the harlot 'under every grove-tree,' we too commit adultery with the wood.

'And faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in a lie.' (John 10:16) If we have turned to God, but deficiently, we are accused as not having turned 'with the whole heart.' Therefore 'faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart.' He did not say: and faithless Judah turned, and she stood; but: 'and faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in a lie' she turned.

True turning, then, is to read the old things, to know those who were justified, to imitate them; to read those things, to see those who were blamed, to guard ourselves from falling into those blames; to read the books of the new covenant, the words of the apostles; after reading, to write all these things into the heart, to live according to them, so that a bill of divorce may not be given to us also, but that we may be able to come to the holy inheritance, and that, the fullness of the nations having been saved, Israel may then be able to enter. For if the fullness of the nations enters, then all Israel will be saved, 'and they shall become one flock, one shepherd,' teaching to glorify the almighty God in Christ Jesus himself, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

before: He adds: 'And nations will bless themselves in him, and in him they will praise God in Jerusalem. For thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem.' (Genesis 12:3; 18:18; 22:18; 26:4) He has spoken to those from the nations, and he has spoken to those from Israel; he speaks to those from Judah. I remember the figurative readings said earlier about Judah and those dwelling in Jerusalem. For we dwell—if God grants—in Jerusalem.

Since 'where the treasure is, there the heart is also,' (Galatians 4:26) if we store up treasure in heaven, we also have the heart in the Jerusalem above, about which the apostle says: 'But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother,' as it is written, and what follows. So 'thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem: Break new ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.' (Jeremiah 4:3) This word is spoken especially to those who teach, so that they not entrust what is said to the hearers before they make new ground in their souls. For when, putting hand to the plow, they make new ground in souls—according to the good and fine soil of those who hear—then as they sow they do not sow among thorns.

But if, before the plow and before making new ground in the ruling principle of the hearers, someone takes the holy seeds—the word about the Father, about the Son, about the Holy Spirit, about resurrection, about punishment, about rest, about law, about prophets, and in short about each of the things written—and sows them, he transgresses the command that says first, 'Break new ground for yourselves,' and second, 'Do not sow among thorns.'

But one of the hearers will say: 'I do not teach; I am not under this command.' You too become a farmer of yourself, and do not sow among thorns, but make new ground for me in the plot God of all has entrusted to you. Consider the plot; see where the thorns are—where cares of life and deceit of wealth and love of pleasure are. Having seen the thorns in your soul, seek the rational plow about which Jesus says, 'No one who puts hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of God.' Having sought it and found it, gathering from the Scriptures the pure working oxen, plow and renew the land, and so that it may no longer be old, make it new—putting off the old man with his practices and putting on the new man renewed into knowledge. You will make new ground for yourself, and if you make the new ground, take seeds from those who teach, take seeds from the law, from the prophets, from the Gospel writings, from the apostolic words, and having taken these seeds sow the soul through memory and study. They will seem to spring up of themselves; but in truth after the memory of them it is not they that spring up, but God who grows them: 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.' (1 Corinthians 3:6) And if anyone has been able to understand the Scriptures, that one has made new ground, and having made it has sown not among thorns. These seeds are managed by God not to become an ear all at once, but as in the Gospel according to Mark: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain.

When it is ready for harvest, those sent out upon the harvest will come. When it is ready for harvest, they will come to whom the word says: 'Lift up your eyes and see the fields, that they are already white for harvest.' So he says to us: 'Break new ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.' But if, before you cleanse your soul, while you still have thorns, you approach one who can teach or is thought to teach, or ask for lessons and spiritual seeds, you transgress the command that says, 'Do not sow among thorns.'

before: 'I was sitting alone.' And the words are managed here. Whenever there is a multitude of sinners and they do not bear the righteous living righteously, it is not out of place for one fleeing the council of wickedness to imitate the one who said: 'I was sitting alone,' to imitate also Elijah who says: 'Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my soul to take it.' (1 Kings 19:10, 14) And perhaps even if you examine more deeply 'I was sitting alone,' you will find some mind worthy of prophetic depth. Whenever we imitate the life of the many, so as not to be withdrawn and better and exceptional beside the many, I cannot say: 'I was sitting alone,' but: I was sitting with many.

But when my life becomes hard to imitate, so that I become so great that no one is near me in character, in word, in deeds, in wisdom, then I can say—because of being alone such and no one imitating me—'I was sitting alone.'

So it is possible even if you are not an elder and not a bishop and not honored with some church honor to say this, to zealously imitate 'I was sitting alone' and take up a life so as to say: 'I was sitting alone.' 'Because I was filled with bitternesses.' (1 Kings 19:10) If 'narrow and afflicted is the way,' how does your feast come to be with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says 'you shall eat unleavened breads upon bitter herbs.' (Exodus 12:8; Num 9:11) What the word wants saying that the one feasting to God must eat 'unleavened breads upon bitter herbs' (Galatians 4:16) must be considered. The apostle interpreted the unleavened breads; the interpretation is not mine; but what follows of the interpretation must necessarily be near the apostolic interpretation.

The apostle interpreted the things about the unleavened breads saying: 'Let us feast not in old leaven nor in leaven of wickedness and evil, but in unleavened breads of sincerity and truth.' (1 Corinthians 5:8) It is necessary to give the account about the bitter herbs following upon the unleavened breads being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you eat with bitter herbs the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth—as Paul. Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.' (2 Corinthians 11:27–28)

So the law said: 'You shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs'; and it did not say: you shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs until you are filled, as upon certain other things it has been said: 'You shall eat and be filled.' But the prophet presses further saying that I did not eat bitterness, but 'I was filled with bitternesses'; as much strength as there was I partook of bitter affairs, so as to partake with the fullest bitter herbs.

before: Because “his yoke is kind and the burden light.” (Lamentations 3:27–28) Let no one assent with him about something; one must not be led away together, but even if he is isolated toward this, to endure in what has been decided and to be firmly settled. For “the Lord settles mono-way ones in a house,” (Matthew 11:30) says David, and “I am alone until I pass by” (Psalm 68:6)—clearly the trials, having obtained kindness (Psalm 141:10).

before: Then I want to say something else from the Scripture itself.

Samuel comes up, and what does the woman say to Saul she has seen? She does not say she has seen a human; she shrank before this one she saw. Whom does she see? “I have seen gods,” she says, “gods coming up from the earth.” And perhaps Samuel has not come up alone then also to prophesy to Saul; but likely—just as here “with a holy one you will be made holy, and with a blameless man you will be blameless, and with a chosen one you will be chosen,” (1 Samuel 28:13) and there are here sojourns of holy ones with holy ones, not of holy ones with sinners, and if ever, the holy ones’ sojourn with sinners is for saving the sinners too—so perhaps as Samuel came up there also came up with him either other prophets’ holy souls or angels who had come up with the spirits. Perhaps you will ask whether angels were upon their spirits? The prophet says: “the angel who speaks in me”; and everything is filled with those who need salvation, and “all are ministering spirits sent for service because of those about to inherit salvation.” (Psalm 18:25–26)

Why fear to say that every place needs Jesus Christ? The one who needs Christ needs the prophets; for he does not need Christ while not needing those who prepare Christ’s presence and sojourn. And John—than whom no one greater among those born of women, according to our Savior’s witness saying, “Among those born of women none is greater than John the Baptist” (Zechariah 1:9)—do not fear to say that he has gone down into Hades proclaiming my Lord beforehand, so that he may foretell him as about to come down. For this reason, when he was in prison and knew the departure lying upon him, sending two of his disciples he inquired—not “Are you the one who is coming?” (for he knew)—but “Are you the one who is coming, or should we expect another?” (Hebrews 1:14) He saw his glory; he spoke many things about his wonder; he first bore him witness: “He who comes after me has come to be before me” (Matthew 11:11); he saw his glory, glory as of an only-begotten from a father, full of grace and truth. Having seen such things about Christ he hesitates to believe, doubts, and does not say: “Tell him, ‘You are the Christ.’” For now some, not understanding what was said, say: “John so great did not know Christ, but the Holy Spirit stood away from him.” (Matthew 11:3) And he knew this one to whom he bore witness before birth and over whom he leaped when Mary also came to him, as his mother bore him witness saying: “For behold, when the sound of your greeting came into my ears, the baby leaped in exultation in my womb.” (John 1:15, 27, 30–34)

This John, then, who leaped before birth, who said, “This is he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has come to be before me,’” (John 1:14) and “He who sent me said to me, ‘He on whom you see the Spirit coming down and remaining, this is the Son of God’” (Luke 1:41–44)—this one, they say, no longer knew Jesus Christ? For in the womb he knew him. But through excess of glory he has done something like Peter. What like? This one knew something great about Christ. “Who am I? Whom do people say I am?” And he: such and such. And you? “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:13–17)—for which he is also blessed, because “flesh and blood did not reveal” it to him, “but the Father in the heavens.”

Since therefore he heard great things about Christ and supposed great things and did not accept the divine word toward him—“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and it will be finished,” (Matthew 16:21–22) and “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the chief priests and elders, and be killed, and on the third day rise”—he says, “Mercy to you, Lord.” He knew great things about Christ; he did not want to accept the more humble thing about him. Think of John as some such person for me. He was in prison knowing great things about Christ; he saw heavens opened; he saw the Holy Spirit coming down from heaven upon the Savior and remaining on him; seeing such glory he doubted and perhaps disbelieved whether the one so glorious would also go down as far as Hades and as far as the abyss; for this reason he said: “Are you the one who is coming, or should we expect another?”

For 'Woe to those who laugh now, for they will mourn and weep' (Matthew 5:8)—one weeping is the blessed, another is stored up for those who have lived badly. The Gospel bears witness when it narrates the things about the Samaritan woman; for there the same is named 'spring' and 'well,' and by turns it is sometimes called spring and sometimes well. This is a preface for me of the narration about to come, because of the clay vessel that fell apart from the potter’s hand and was molded again. Let this narration also have its grace.

before: This prophetic word is more properly referred to the Savior. Grant that the prophet says it; yet he will not say it truly, but perhaps by exaggeration—for he was not examined against all the earth. But if I come to my Savior and Lord, and especially because he will come to judgment, and because of the word 'that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged,' (Psalm 51:6) I will see that my Savior and Lord is about to stand before the Father, being judged with all of us humans. And he is judged with all humans. I mean: he is judged, he himself is examined, and he stood defending the truth—not as an accuser. 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth?' (Jeremiah 20:15) A prophet cannot say 'in all the earth.'

But some who love the Lord are also angry and say that the Savior does not speak this, that the voice is not fitting for the Son of God. Yet one must show that 'Woe is me, mother' is not alien to the Son of God: 'My soul is very sorrowful unto death,' (Matthew 26:38) and 'My soul is troubled,' and of the things said in the prophets likewise also here: 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth' (Micah 7:1–2)—or when the gleaning has failed for finding a cluster: 'Woe is me, soul, for the godly one has perished from the earth, and the one who acts uprightly among men does not exist.'

Who says there, 'Woe, for I became as one gathering stubble in harvest'? Does the prophet gather, and want to gather? Does the prophet have a field? But it belongs to no one to gather everything from the harvest and from what was sown, except the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Since therefore there are many falls among the nations, and also sins among us, he says: 'Woe is me, for I became as one gathering stubble.' Let each of us examine himself: is he an ear of grain? Will the Son of God find in him something to glean or to harvest? We will find that some of us are wind-blasted; and if we still have a little in ourselves—two or three grains—our sins are many upon us.

Seeing then also the churches that are so called, filled with sinners, he says: 'Woe, for I became as one gathering stubble in harvest and as a gleaning in vintage.' He comes, and seeks somehow to glean; he finds some gleaning and short clusters, not flourishing and not many. Which of us has clusters of virtue? Which of us has offspring of God?

before: I move from the letter—though I have already taken the road the word gave—onto each soul already counted worthy to see peace. For after the divine lessons you have become Jerusalem, having formerly been Jebus. History says that one's name was Jebus; then second it changed the name and it became Jerusalem. Children of the Hebrews say Jebus is interpreted 'Trodden.'

So Jebus—the soul trodden by opposing powers—has been changed and has become Jerusalem, Vision of peace. If then, when you changed from Jebus so as to become Jerusalem, you sinned and trampled the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant common (as that Jerusalem did, and you too) and are in hard sins, it will be said also about you: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?' (Hebrews 10:29)—if you become such as to betray Jesus. Each of us, when we sin—and especially if the sins are greater—sins against Jesus.

And if one is also an apostate, still more does he do to Jesus spiritually what Jerusalem did to him bodily. Therefore: 'How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled the Son of God and counted common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?' (Hebrews 6:4–5) If you have trampled the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace, who 'will spare you? Who will look gloomy over you? Who will turn back to ask after the things that make for your peace?' (Hebrews 6:6) The sinner's soul has betrayed the very Son of God who asked after the things that make for your peace. Who can turn back again and plead concerning peace? Knowing then that 'it is impossible to renew again to repentance those who were once enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift and became partakers of the Holy Spirit and tasted the good word of God and powers of the age to come, and fell away, crucifying again in themselves the Son of God and making a spectacle of him,' let us do everything so that it may not also be said about us: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? after: I move from the letter—though I have already taken the road the word gave—onto each soul already counted worthy to see peace. For after the divine lessons you have become Jerusalem, having formerly been Jebus. History says that one's name was Jebus; then second it changed the name and it became Jerusalem. Children of the Hebrews say Jebus is interpreted 'Trodden.'

So Jebus—the soul trodden by opposing powers—has been changed and has become Jerusalem, Vision of peace. If then, when you changed from Jebus so as to become Jerusalem, you sinned and trampled the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant common (as that Jerusalem did, and you too) and are in hard sins, it will be said also about you: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?' (Jeremiah 15:5)—if you become such as to betray Jesus. Each of us, when we sin—and especially if the sins are greater—sins against Jesus.

And if one is also an apostate, still more does he do to Jesus spiritually what Jerusalem did to him bodily. Therefore: 'How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled the Son of God and counted common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?' before: Some stories do not touch us; some are necessary for our hope. I have said “stories” (Psalm 99:6–7) thus, since we do not yet arrive at the things of the ascent—useful to everyone who knows how to ascend or to hear those who ascend. Of the things of the story, then, some are useful to all, some not to all. For example: the story concerning Lot and his daughters—if it has something useful according to the ascent, God knows, and the one to whom he grants to examine those words; but if according to the story, you might ask: what benefit to me from the story concerning Lot and his daughters? Likewise what benefit to me is the story of Judah and Tamar and the things about her, simply told?

But since the story that has Saul and the medium touches everyone, a necessary truth according to the Word. For who, released from this life, wants to be under a demon’s authority, so that a medium may bring up not some chance believer but Samuel the prophet?—of whom God says through Jeremiah: “Even if Moses and Samuel stood before my face, I would not listen even to them” (Genesis 19:30–38); of whom the prophet says in hymns: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call on his name; they called on the Lord, and he himself listened to them; in a pillar of cloud he spoke to them” (Jeremiah 15:1); and elsewhere: “If Moses and Samuel stood…” and what follows.

Therefore—if so great a man was under the earth and the medium brought him up—does a demon have authority over a prophetic soul? What shall we say? These things are written: are they true, or are they not true? To say they are not true drives toward unbelief—it will come down on the heads of those who say it. But to say they are true supplies us with inquiry and difficulty.

before: Upon these things God says concerning Israel: 'If Israel turns to me, says the Lord, he will also turn'—that is, if he turns completely, he will turn with a turning, not if he merely begins, as it were, to turn. Then he says: 'And if he removes his abominations from his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears, “As the Lord lives,” in truth and in judgment and in righteousness, then nations will bless themselves in him.'

If they do these things, 'nations will bless themselves in him.' (Jeremiah 4:1) What must they do so that nations bless themselves in him? 'If he removes his abominations from his mouth.' (Jeremiah 4:4) What is removing abominations from the mouth? Whatever we speak badly are abominations in our mouth. So let us remove the abominations from our mouth, taking away slanders, empty words, idle words that will make us answerable on the day of judgment—'for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.' (Matthew 12:37)

Next is also, 'You will stand in awe before my face.' Let us do this second thing, not simply so that we may be reverent. For there can be a reverence that does not come from the face of God. Those who fear without knowledge, though they propose to fear, do not stand in awe from the face of God. But as many as stand in awe with knowledge—by always looking and painting for themselves the face of God that comes upon those who do evil, to wipe out their memory from the earth—these are the ones who stand in awe from the face of God.

before: Then there is another prophecy, which somehow we did not find among the Seventy, but we found in the remaining editions—clearly lying in the Hebrew—and it is filled with most necessary matters that can, if we pay attention, turn our soul back. The words run thus: 'The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with an adamant point upon the breast of their heart.' (Jeremiah 17:1)

It is easier to give oneself over and say: These things are written about the Jews, that their sin 'is written.' But if you see, as we have often shown, Judah spoken tropically as Christ, perhaps 'the sin of Judah' is ours—of those who believe upon Christ who is from the tribe of Judah. And if you can also hear it more mystically another way, perhaps it prophesies about Judas who handed him over, so that the prophecy about him says: 'The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with an adamant point upon the breast of the heart.' (Luke 8:17 || Matt 10:26) But again 'their' does not follow for that one. Perhaps then he was speaking upon us: if we become sinners, these prophesied things reach us.

We have sinned, and our sin is not written outside us, but in our heart, and it is written 'with an iron pen, with an adamant point.' (1 Corinthians 4:5) That the sins we commit are inscribed into us by the sinning, the matter itself will show. I did not know this deed or this sin in myself; having done it I have its imprint, and as it were the imprint of my committed sin has been written in my soul. And if my sin had been written with ink, I would have wiped it away; but now it is written 'with an iron pen,' written 'with an adamant point,' written 'upon the breast of our heart,' so that I may come to the place of teaching and the prophecy that says may be fulfilled: 'Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, and nothing covered that will not be revealed.' (Isaiah 46:10 || Acts 15:18) My breast was stripped bare, and the heart holding the written letters of the sin—'with the pen upon my breast and in my heart the imprints of my sins.' For 'nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest.'
From these things may the God of all deliver us, that we may rise into the glory that is in Christ, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages. Amen.

before: 'Behold, they say to me: Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come. But I did not grow weary following after you.' (Matthew 16:24) Jesus says to you: 'Take up your cross and follow me,' and 'Leave all things and follow me,' and 'Whoever does not leave father and mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple.' (Matthew 19:21) If then you become such that you always follow Jesus, you will also follow, and as long as you follow you will not grow weary; for 'there will be no toil in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel.' (Matthew 10:37–38) There is no labor for the one following Jesus; the very following takes away the labor.

Therefore he himself says, so that we may no longer grow weary—having grown weary before we began to follow him: 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' (Matthew 11:28) If then, laboring, we come to him and follow him, we will say: 'But I did not grow weary following after you.'

And it is consequent for us to say also: 'I did not desire a human day.' There is a day of a human, and there is a day of God. Let each of us desire the day of the resurrection of the holy ones, not that day concerning which it is written: 'Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; and this is darkness and not light.' Who is the one who says: 'And I did not desire a human day'? The clarity of the word will convict us that we have desired a human day. Often when we have fallen sick and come into a fantasy of death, at the departure we beg the brothers who watch over us and say: Ask for me a leave, ask for me to remain in life. Saying these things we do not desire a holy day of God, but a human day. Therefore putting away love of the body and the desire for a human day, let us seek to see that day in which we will obtain the blessedness in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages. Amen.

before: I consider that for us also such things may be, and some punishments may occur, so that these may not have a second punishment but be satisfied with the first, others may come even to the second, not indeed to the third, others may come even to the fourth. For the 'I will add seven plagues' (Jeremiah 5:18) signifies a mystery of one by one being inflicted, and the second, and the third, up to the seven mentioned for some. Not all are struck with seven plagues; rather, some I suppose will be struck with seven, others with five, others with four, others with three or two, and the most helpless among all in punishments I consider to be struck with one. Therefore, God knows the things regarding the plagues. Hence it is written here at the beginning of the reading: 'And it will be in those days... I will not make an end for you. Not an end in those days; for there are some days when He will make those He wills for an end.' (Leviticus 26:18)

before: And something most paradoxical Jerusalem suffered at the time of the captivity. For she beheld nations—which God commanded not to enter into the assembly—treading the sanctuary, where not even for the Israelites is it lawful to enter, only the priests having been counted worthy to be in that place after not ordinary purifications. And the enemies reached even as far as the untrodden places, entering into a place which scarcely, after much sanctification, the high priest entered once a year.

And after a little: And if Jerusalem, just as we set out before, is such a soul, one must understand her goods according to nature—being her adornment, through which she was serving the divine—laid away in her places untrodden by everyone except the high-priest Word, to be called her desirable things. And upon all these the enemy who has conquered in wrestling, having afflicted the one not campaigning well for herself but worthily left behind by the divine help, having stretched himself through his operative power unto the base things, has pulled them out of the ruling part and has left desolate of the good things the soul that stood away from God. And nations in this place must be allegorized as the crowd of vices, having entered into the ruling part created to be receptive of God and a true sanctuary of the one wanting to rest upon a pure mind. Which nations God forbids altogether to enter into the church; for what else would we more properly suppose God forbids to enter into a soul numbered in the church of God than the works and the mindset of the flesh, truly being nations hostile to God? “For the flesh campaigns against the spirit,” (Galatians 5:17) “the mindset of the flesh being enmity unto God” (Romans 8:7); “for it is not subject to the law of God; for it is not even able.” (Hebrews 9:7) (Galatians 5:17) (Romans 8:7)

before: Let us begin from: 'A partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear.' (John 10:27) Therefore the devil does not gather his own creatures; he does not gather what he begot; but when he calls, he gathers another’s creatures and makes them his own. A partridge called through Valentinus; a partridge called through Marcion; it called through Basilides, through all the heterodox. For none of those could speak the voice of Jesus: 'My sheep will hear my voice.' But the voice of Jesus is in Paul and Peter; therefore Paul said: 'Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?' (2 Corinthians 13:3)

But the voice of the partridge that gathered what it did not bear is in those who lead astray and deceive, through their simplicity and lack of preparation, the simpler among the believers. Therefore 'a partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear, making its wealth not with judgment.' The partridge grew rich. See how many myriads are his; many have become the partridge’s—of the opposing power. And he made his wealth not caring about judgment and not having judgment, but acting without judgment. Therefore it is said that the partridge is 'making its wealth not with judgment.' But my Savior makes his wealth with judgment, and his wealth is judged and chosen.

before: The enchanters of the Egyptians also had rods that wanted to refute the rods of Moses and Aaron as not being from God. But the rods from God overturn those of the sophists and enchanters; 'Aaron’s swallowed them'—for it alone was enough for this even without Moses’ rod. So then Pashhur 'struck Jeremiah the prophet,' and with character: 'and he struck Jeremiah the prophet.' (Jeremiah 20:2) 'The prophet' is also added. Here then the one who struck Jeremiah the prophet.

And it is written in Acts that someone struck Paul, ordered by Ananias the high priest. Therefore Paul said: 'God is about to strike you, whitewashed wall.' (Acts 23:3) And until now Ebionites, ordered by an unlawful high-priestly word, strike the apostle of Jesus Christ with blasphemous words. And Paul says toward such a high-priestly word: 'God is about to strike you.' And such a high priest is handsome on the surface and a whitewashed wall.

Christ says: 'I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spit.' (Isaiah 53:7) The simple know these things only of that time when Pilate scourged him, when Jews planned against him. But I see Jesus daily 'giving his back to scourges.' before: And next to this it is said: 'Be circumcised to your God; circumcise the foreskin of your heart.' (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jer 4:4) 'Be circumcised to your God'—necessarily is added 'to your God.' You will understand it from the sensible example. According to the sensible I say: not only those of the circumcision according to Moses' (Ephesians 2:3) law are circumcised, but many others also. The priests of the Egyptians' idols are circumcised, but that circumcision is circumcision to idols and is not circumcision done to God. The Jews' circumcision, perhaps—and certainly then—was done to God.

So when the word says, 'Be circumcised to your God,' understand the saying and move also to the figurative reading, so that you find how, among figurative circumcisions (so that some of them might even say, 'We are the circumcision'), some are circumcised to God, and others are circumcised, yet not to God. There are also other words besides the word of truth, besides the word of the church. Those who philosophize chastise manners and the heart, and those from the heresies chastise, and circumcision happens for them. But it is circumcision, yet not to God; for circumcision happens among them by a false word.

But when according to the church's rule, according to the aim of sound teaching, you are in communion, you are not only circumcised—you are circumcised 'to God.' So 'Be circumcised to your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart.' (Philippians 3:21) Who does not pass these words by as clear? So there is a foreskin of the heart, and this must be circumcised.

The one who works the word carefully, searching such things in this place, will examine: foreskin is born with us; circumcision is acquired; and what has come from birth, circumcision removes. If then the word commands the foreskin of the heart to be removed, there must be something born with the heart which he calls foreskin, which must be removed so that someone may be circumcised as to the foreskin of the heart. If anyone understands, 'We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest' (Ephesians 2:3; Prov 20:9); if anyone understands 'the body of our humiliation' in which we were born; if anyone understands, 'No one is clean from filth, not even if his life is one day; his months are numbered'—he will see how we were born with uncleanness and with the foreskin of our heart.

before: 'And your word will be to me for gladness.' (Matthew 23:38) It is not now, but 'it will be'; for upon the present your word is to me for imprisonments, for lawsuits, for affairs, for ill repute, for toils, but the end of these will be gladness. 'And your word will be to me for gladness and joy of my heart, because your name has been called upon me, Lord Almighty.' (Jeremiah 15:16) Even if Christ says it, the Father's name has been called upon him. 'I did not sit in their council of those playing.' (2 Corinthians 6:18) If ever the prophet saw the council not of those serious but of those playing, he fled rather gathering than hastened upon a synagogue of those playing. So you must understand a difference between a council of those playing and of those serious. This council is serious and does everything with seriousness and things worthy of seriousness and according to what is said: seriousness is the word, seriousness is the life, and everywhere the council is not of those playing but of those serious.

But when the council, leaving the seriousness about what is necessary, has leisure for the games of this age and games from wickedness, it becomes a council of those playing. So this one says: 'I did not sit in their council of those playing, but I was cautious from before your hand.' (John 5:43) Two things being set before me—to sit in a council of those playing and to stumble against you God and not please you, or to rise from a council of those playing and do the things that were dear to you—I chose rather to stand up from the council of those playing and be a friend to you than, doing the contrary, to become an enemy to your blessedness. 'I did not sit in their council of those playing, but I was cautious from before your hand.' And our Savior did not sit 'in their council of those playing,' but stood away from them. And a sign that the Savior has been raised from a council of those playing is his having said: 'Your house is left to you desolate.' For the Word of God has left the Jews' council and made for himself another council and church—the one from the nations.

before: The wording of the passage just read has something unclear in it. Let that be understood first; and after that, if God gives, we shall know his hidden intent.

He wants us to know that, as it is written in the Books of Kingdoms, the people was divided in the days of Rehoboam into the kingdom of the ten tribes under Jeroboam and the kingdom of two tribes under Rehoboam. Those under Jeroboam were called Israel, and those under Rehoboam Judah. This division of the people has remained, as far as the history goes, until now. We do not know a history that has gathered Israel and Judah into one.

Israel sinned first, and more — the Israel under Jeroboam and his successors — and sinned so far beyond Judah that they were condemned by providence to become captives to the Assyrians, as the Scripture says, 'until this day.' After that the sons of Judah also sinned, and were condemned as captives to Babylon, not 'until this day' as Israel was, but for seventy years, of which Jeremiah prophesied, and of which Daniel also made mention.

If we take these things of that people then, look at the prophet's words and see whether they do not show something of this kind. He accuses the sins of Israel, and says that when so many sins had come to be for Israel, the congregation of Judah heard their falls, and in what way he had made them captives, and was not trained by it, but added to the sins, so that by the addition, when the sins were compared with the sins of Israel, righteousness was found in Israel rather than in Judah.

Then the prophet is commanded to prophesy, as of Judah being worse than Israel, so that after the sins Judah may turn. After the prophecy toward Israel commanding him to turn, the prophet prophesies that Israel and Judah are going to become together, and that there will sometime be one kingdom of both. Let the one who cares for the readings take the words of the whole reading today, and then he will see the thoughts laid out.

And the Lord said to me in the days of Josiah the king: 'Have you seen what the dwelling of Israel has done to me' (Jeremiah 3:6) — not Judah, but Israel first? 'She went upon every high mountain and under every leafy tree and played the harlot there. And I said after she had done all these things: Turn back to me. And she did not turn. And faithless Judah saw the faithlessness of the congregation of Israel.' (2 Kings 17:6) And those from Judah saw that, for all the things in which the dwelling of Israel committed adultery, 'I sent her away and gave her a bill of divorce.' (Jeremiah 3:8) Judah ought to have been trained — for I sent Israel away, I threw them out to the Assyrians, and I gave her a bill of divorce into her hands — 'and faithless Judah was not afraid.' (Daniel 9:2)

After so many things that I did to Israel, sending him away, giving a bill of divorce, the congregation of Judah ought to have been trained by what those others suffered. They were not only not trained, but they added to the sins, so that the sins of the congregation of Israel, compared with the sins of the congregation of Judah, seem to be righteousness. 'And I gave her a bill of divorce into her hands, and her sister, faithless Judah, was not afraid, and she went and played the harlot also, and her harlotry came to nothing, and she committed adultery with the wood and the stone. And in all these things faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in a lie.' (Jeremiah 3:6–11)

She was not ashamed before me of what I had done to Israel, that she might turn completely. She ought to have turned in truth, and she turned in a lie. And the Lord said to me: 'Israel has justified her soul from faithless Judah.' The sins of Israel, compared with the falls of Judah, have become a justification of the soul of the congregation of Israel.

before: So that those who were fished and afterward came into the mountains may not suppose that these things have come to them from righteousness, the word reminds not only them but also us of the former sins. Therefore after the benefits it is said: 'And their injustices were not hidden before my eyes.' (Jeremiah 2:22 or Jer 16:17)

What follows is about to put a contest before us. For if we understand it as following, we will take careful thought about the repayment of the sins; and if it seems not to follow what was set out before about those being fished and hunted, even so it throws us into no small contest. For he says: 'And I will repay first double their injustices and their sins, with which they profaned my land in the carcasses of the abominations and by their lawless deeds with which they filled my inheritance.' (Jeremiah 16:18) Whether some, not understanding, removed the 'first' from what is written, or the Seventy managed to remove it, God would know. But we, comparing with the remaining editions, found it lying there: 'And I will repay first double their injustices,' (cf. Matt 9:2, 6; Mark 2:5, 10; Luke 5:20, 24) so that it may be shown that even if through their second works they were worthy of blessedness, since they are humans and have come to be in sins, they must first receive their sins.

And see whether the word is not true. Who will not receive the sins—except the one who, after believing and receiving forgiveness of sins (so as to hear Jesus say: 'Your sins are forgiven you'), no longer sins? But if after the forgiveness of sins and the economy of the washing of regeneration we sin—as we the many do, who have not been perfected like the apostles—and after sinning, and while sinning, also do some things that are due, what awaits us must be considered. If we leave life holding sins and also holding brave deeds, will we be saved through the brave deeds and released concerning the things we sinned in knowledge? Or will we be punished through the sins and nowhere receive a wage for the brave deeds? before: 'And I said, You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am younger. And the Lord said to me, Do not say that I am younger, because to all to whom I send you...' (Jeremiah 1:6–8) We have often said that it is possible, according to the inner man, to be a child, even if someone is in an old age of body. And it is possible at times, according to the outer man, to be a child, and according to the inner, a man. Such was Jeremiah, already having the grace from God while he was still in the age of a child according to the body. That is why the Lord says to him, 'Do not say that I am younger.' (Jeremiah 1:7) And a sign that he is not younger, but 'a grown man,' is this: 'To all to whom I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face.' (Matthew 13:57)

The Word of God knows that those who serve as ambassadors of the word are in danger among the hearers. For when they are exposed they hate them; when they are rebuked they persecute them. The prophets suffer every kind of thing. 'A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his house' (Jeremiah 38:6–9) — which we also recalled earlier. So God, sending the prophet, knows how many dangers he will take on, and he says to him, 'Do not be afraid of their face, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 1:8)

What Jeremiah suffered is written down. He was thrown into a pit of mire; he remained there eating one loaf a day and drinking water only; and ten thousand other things which his prophecy has made clear. 'Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?' (Acts 7:52) it is said to the Jews. And it is necessary that 'those who want to live in a godly way in Christ Jesus be persecuted in every case by opposing powers, through the vessels they find.' (2 Timothy 3:12) Therefore those who are persecuted must not be surprised, but must do everything, only praying that they be persecuted unjustly and not justly — not for injustice, not for sin, not for greed. And if someone is ever persecuted for righteousness, let him also hear, 'Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil word against you, lying, for my sake (Matthew 5:11). Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is great in the heavens; for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.' (Matthew 5:10–12) (2 Corinthians 4:16)

before: Then, after many words have gone by, it would indeed have been necessary to speak about each of the things said; but there is no room, with time pressing on. Let us therefore speak to what follows, taking up: 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' (Jeremiah 17:5) From those who suppose that the Son of God, the Savior, was merely a man—for they dared, along with many human evils, to say also this, that there is no God who is 'the only-begotten,' 'the firstborn of all creation'—'cursed' is 'the one who has his hope upon a man.' It is clear that those who have their hope upon a man are under a curse.

I would say that I do not have my hope upon a man. Hoping upon Christ Jesus, I do not know a man. Not only do I not know a man, but I know Wisdom, absolute Righteousness, the one through whom 'all things were created' among the authorities. 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' (2 Corinthians 5:16) Even if the Savior bears witness that what he wore was a man—yet even if he was a man, now he is in no way a man. For 'if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet we know him so no longer,' (2 Corinthians 5:16) says the apostle. Through him I am no longer a man, if I follow his words; but he says: 'I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.' Therefore, as he is 'firstborn from the dead,' so he has become firstborn of all humans by changing them toward God.

'Cursed,' then, 'is the man who has his hope upon a man, and will strengthen the flesh of his arm'—whoever ratifies the fleshly things, whoever acquires bodily strength and campaigns according to the flesh. But the holy one is not like that: for 'he does not strengthen the flesh of his arm,' for he 'always' has 'the dying of Jesus in his body,' and he puts to death 'the members that are upon the earth—fornication, uncleanness.' Having put these to death, 'he does not strengthen the flesh of his arm.'

'Cursed is the one who has his hope upon a man.' And at the same time this is said toward those who hope in dignities. So-and-so is my friend; he is a centurion, he is a steward; so-and-so is my friend and is rich and supplies me. Then toward such a person also this is said: 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' We hope upon no human being, even if they seem to be our friends; for we do not hope upon them but upon our Lord, who is Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages of ages. Amen.

before: First one must speak about the 'woe'—whether because of its ill-sounding character the Savior can say 'woe,' he who also pronounces woes on others. We will set out from agreed sayings, which fit no one but the Savior, how he also wept over Jerusalem; and the voice of one weeping is 'woe.' And it lies in the Gospel that seeing Jerusalem he wept over it and said: 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather your children,' (Luke 19:41) and what follows. And clearly these too were spoken by the Savior in the 'Woe that I became as one gathering stubble in harvest and as gleaning in vintage, there being no ear to eat the firstfruits. Woe, soul, that the devout has perished from the earth, and the one who walks upright among humans does not exist. All are judged for bloodshed.' (Matthew 23:37)
For he came as one gathering stubble into a harvest in order to reap, and finds many sinners and says: 'Woe that I became as one gathering stubble in harvest.' (Job 16:20 or similar lament)

He came to vintage fruit of life among humans; he finds many sins in us and for this reason says: 'And as gleaning in vintage, there being no ear to eat the firstfruits.' And elsewhere he says something near these things to the Father: 'What benefit is there in my blood, in my going down into corruption?' What great benefit have I given humans? What worthy of the blood which I poured out for them have they done? 'What benefit is there in my blood, in my going down' from heavens? I have gone down; I came upon the earth; I gave myself over to corruption; I wore a human body; what worthy of them has been set right for humans? 'What benefit is there in my blood, in my going down into corruption? Will dust confess you, or announce your truth?' Such then is also what is said here first by the Savior: 'Woe is me, mother, as whom did you bear me, a man?' Not as God does the Savior say 'Woe is me, mother,' but as human, as in the prophet: 'Woe, soul, that the devout has perished from the earth.'

And the soul was human; for this reason it was also troubled, for this reason it was also deeply grieved. But the Word who was in the beginning with God is not troubled; that one would not say 'woe.' For the Word does not admit death, but it is the human that admitted this, as we have often set out.

before: But I found one hole of one rock; I move in the word from the hole to the cleft of the rock, and I seek also the many rocks. If I come to the choir—whether of the prophets or of the apostles or even of holy angels who have gone up higher—I say that all who imitate Christ, as he is a rock, become rocks. And just as he has a hole through which God’s back parts are contemplated, in the same way each one, giving a way for God to be understood through the things said by him, makes a hole in himself—or if you wish to name it otherwise, a cleft.

From that hole or cleft you will see through Moses the law, through Isaiah his prophecy, through Jeremiah other words of God. before: 'Shame,' then, 'has consumed the labors of our fathers from their youth—their sheep and their oxen.' (Exodus 13:2, 12–15; Numbers 3:13; 8:17) What is there in us that is tilling us—whether tilling badly (so that 'badly' is said of the tiller) or tilling well? If it tills badly, that is labor of the fathers being consumed by their shame. If it tills well, it is not the fathers' labor, but labor from which the firstborn are offered upon God's altar. They say 'their sons and their daughters.' (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27; cf. John 1:12–13; Romans 8:14–16) Whose 'their'? Are the sons of 'them' or of 'the fathers' consumed by their shame? And we have often said that the offspring of the soul are these: thoughts are sons, and the works and bodily practices are daughters.

Since there are wicked thoughts—such as those from the nations thought—and wicked works as well, sons and daughters are consumed by those who made them, if shame arises in them over what was sinned. May it not be that we make sons and daughters for a consumption that comes from shame.

before: According to the bodily narrative what is said about Jerusalem now is such. Uncleanness is an obstacle for Jerusalem; but of what it is an obstacle, the prophet has left for us to understand. Perhaps it shows that the uncleanness is a hinderer of her journey. And also, being such, it shows that Jerusalem did not remember her last things. And the one who has these before the eyes and sees what will meet him because of the sins will not sin. Because of this uncleanness, then, there is an obstacle for her; and because she does not remember her last things, she brought down her wonderful and great things—which she had when she was worthy to be overseen—and led them into lowliness, though formerly they were oversized and greater than every praise. But also after all these things there was none comforting her: “See, O Lord, my humiliation,” (John 13:7–8) says the speaker, “since the enemy is magnified over what has happened to my homeland.” (Lamentations 1:9)

And after a little: Yet one must inquire, according to the laws of the ascent-sense, whether it is possible for uncleanness to be in someone who is not its cause. And let us also see the first thoughts of the Lament. Such a soul, having fallen away, is altogether also in uncleanness, which uncleanness hinders walking the holy road. And just as holy Moses and his successor Joshua are commanded by God to loose the sandals when stepping upon a holy place—it not being fitting for the feet to wear dead hide in a holy place—so if someone is going to walk unimpeded, perhaps he ought not only to loose but also to wash off the uncleanness that has come about from the dust around the feet. And we suppose a symbol of this to be that the Savior, having put water into the basin, washed the feet of the disciples, saying to Peter who did not yet understand the mystery and for this reason was hindering: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me,” (John 13:8) and “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know after these things.” (John 13:7) Therefore it will be necessary for the uncleanness around the feet of the soul, so to speak, also to need Jesus, so that he may wash it off and we may be able to have a part with him. For if this remains, it is an obstacle to our walking the road according to the sound word—the Savior who said: “I am the way.” (John 14:6)

And just as holy Moses and his successor Joshua are commanded by God to loose the sandals when stepping upon a holy place—it not being fitting for the feet to wear dead hide in a holy place—so if someone is going to walk unimpeded, perhaps he ought not only to loose but also to wash off the uncleanness that has come about from the dust around the feet. And we suppose a symbol of this to be that the Savior, having put water into the basin, washed the feet of the disciples, saying to Peter who did not yet understand the mystery and for this reason was hindering: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me,” (John 13:8) and “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know after these things.” (John 13:7) Therefore it will be necessary for the uncleanness around the feet of the soul, so to speak, also to need Jesus, so that he may wash it off and we may be able to have a part with him. For if this remains, it is an obstacle to our walking the road according to the sound word—the Savior who said: “I am the way.” (John 14:6)

before: They have hardened their faces above the rock; understand this from the more physical. Those who hear reproving words about sin blush and sink down and fall beneath the word of their reprover. But those are such that they are unblushing, not ashamed of what they are reproved for, what they have sinned. Therefore, if you were to speak about those who do not blush, 'They have hardened their faces above the rock,' (Jeremiah 5:3–5) if you have understood this upon the physical, turn with me in the word to the soul's face, about which it is said, 'Then face to face.' And see a firm soul, such as the heart of Pharaoh, hardened so that it stands as a counterpart to what is spoken and as if rejecting what is said, not shaped according to what is spoken.

For there you will find that 'They have hardened their faces above the rock and did not wish to turn back.' (1 Corinthians 13:12) And I said, 'Perhaps they are poor, because they did not wish to know the way of the Lord and the judgment of God.' I will go to the stout and speak to them. before: God is a wilderness to no one, making the sun rise on the evil and on the good; he is untilled land to no one, sending rain on the just and on the unjust. How is he a wilderness, who makes day and night for rest? How is he a wilderness, who makes the earth bear fruit? How is he a wilderness, who orders each soul so that it may be rational, take up knowledge, train its understanding, and have its senses sound? So as to the common account, God is a wilderness to no one.

As to the particular, I come to Israel's affairs and I say: he was neither wilderness nor untilled land when he did the signs and wonders for the people in Egypt. If a time came when they were abandoned, he became, as it were, a wilderness to them, though he himself was not a wilderness.

When he was not a wilderness to Israel, nor untilled land, he was, on the particular account, a wilderness and untilled land to the nations. But when he turned away from Israel, and became to that Israel a wilderness and untilled land, then grace was poured out on the nations, and now Christ Jesus has become to us not a wilderness but full, not untilled land but fruit-bearing. For 'the children of the desolate are more than of her who has a husband.' (Matthew 5:45)

And he threatens those to whom he was not a wilderness nor untilled land, saying: I did not become a wilderness to you, nor untilled land, but you have said, 'We will not be ruled; we will not come to you any more.' (Hebrews 5:14) Did the sons of Israel say this, out of their senses, according to the letter: 'We will not be ruled' (Jeremiah 2:31) (Isaiah 54:1)?

before: That such things will also be ours at the completion of this age is clear from what the Savior said in the Gospel, in which he says: 'Because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of the many will grow cold. But the one who endures to the end, this one will be saved.' (Matthew 24:12–13) And: 'he will do signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.' (Matthew 24:24)

Our affairs will be such that the Savior says about his own coming, as if a faithful one will not quickly be found from so many churches: 'But when the Son of man comes, will he find the faith on the earth?' (Luke 18:8)

And truly, if we judge things by truth and not by crowds, and judge things by choice and not by seeing many gathered, we shall see now that we are not faithful. But they were faithful then, when the noble martyrdoms were taking place, when, having sent the martyrs on from the burial-places, we came to the gatherings, and the whole church arrived uncrushed, and the catechumens were catechized upon the martyrdoms and upon the deaths of those who confessed the truth unto death, not frightened or shaken from the living God. before: Then he teaches, for those who sinned—as far as the wording goes—then in Jerusalem and in Judea, with what sort of wine God fills these wineskins, the sinners. For it is written: 'If they say to you, “Not knowing, we will not know that every wineskin will be filled with wine,” (Jeremiah 5:3) you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Look, I fill all who inhabit this land and the kings sitting as sons of David on his throne and the priests.' The one about to punish spares no one. Not because someone was named a prophet, yet has sins, will he not be filled with the threats spoken. Not because someone was named a priest and seemed to have the superiority of a more honored name than the people does God spare him so that he is not punished when he has sinned. And the things written about those people, the apostle says, were written for us, 'upon whom the ends of the ages have come.' If then anyone among these priests also (I mean us elders) or among these Levites standing around the people (I mean the deacons) sins, he will have this punishment—as again there are certain priestly blessings, about which, God granting, not far off but after the examination of the prophetic word we will know when Numbers is read; for something about priests is about to be said there. So 'the priests' and 'the prophets and Judah and all who inhabit Jerusalem,' God says he will fill 'with drunkenness' and scatter 'them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons.' And let us understand these things thus: God gathers the righteous, but scatters the sinners. Therefore also when human beings had not moved from the east, God did not scatter them; but when they moved 'from the east' and 'a man said to his neighbor: Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose head will be to heaven,' God says about them: 'Come, let us go down and confuse their tongue there,' and each is confused and scattered to some place of the earth. And the people of Israel, when not sinning, was in Judea; but having sinned is scattered afterward throughout the inhabited world and sown everywhere.
Think something of this kind with me also about all of us.

There is a 'church of firstborn enrolled in heaven,' (Hebrews 12:23) where is Mount Zion and city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem. The blessed will be gathered there, that they may be together. But sinners are also punished in this: in not being with one another. I know some in this life who, for punishment, want to hand over to some island and, for torment, the household of someone who grieved the kingdom, scattering—here the wife, here the one son, then elsewhere the other—so that not even in the disaster the mother may enjoy the son, or the brother the brother. Think something of this kind also upon the unjust. You who are a sinner managed by God must taste something more bitter, that being disciplined you may be saved.

And just as you do not punish a household slave or son under your punishment simply wanting to torment him, but that by the pains you may turn him, so also God will discipline those not turned by the word, those not healed, with the pains from sufferings. For discipline he puts around what he puts around according to what is said: 'With toil and scourge you will always be disciplined, Jerusalem.' (Jeremiah 13:14) So that the disciplining pain may grow, those in pain are scattered from one another so that this one and that one may not be together. For the intensity of the pain would be loosened through the comfort of each toward what comes from the other (Ezekiel 20:23).

before: 'If a man will make gods for himself.' (Ezekiel 36:23) Not only from statues do men make gods for themselves, but you will also find them making gods for themselves from moldings of the mind. For as many as can mold another god and another world-making besides the one written up by the Spirit—a management of the world besides the true world—all these have made gods for themselves and have worshiped the works of their hands. Consider, for example, among the Greeks those who generated doctrines of this philosophy or that, or among the heresies those who first generated doctrines: these made idols for themselves and moldings of the soul, and turning they worshiped the works of their hands, accepting their own moldings as truth.

Therefore the word, refuting all who make gods for themselves both sensibly and intelligibly, says: 'If a man will make gods for himself—and these are not gods? For this reason I will show them my hand at this time, and I will make known to them also my power.' At what time, if not this one—pointing to the time of the Lord’s presence? 'And they will know,' he says, 'that my name is Lord.'

before: Next after these he says he became a laugh. Hear the place. Jeremiah came to be in times of people most sinful—for in his days the captivity came to be—and they were so sinful as to sneer and laugh and mock whenever the prophet spoke the prophetic opening, 'Thus says the Lord.' The hearers laughed and sneered at what was said. The one deceived and benefited from being deceived guarded himself from saying 'Thus says the Lord.' Therefore he also, wanting to deceive for benefit from deceiving, said: I speak my own words to you, since you do not hear the Lord’s words. Then they offered their ears as to words of Jeremiah and heard words of God. These things the one who handed the place over to me said, examining the openings and beginnings of the prophecies.

There is then also a beginning of Jeremiah’s prophecy among us, as the Seventy have handed down—I do not know with what aim: 'The word of God which came upon Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah from the priests' (Jeremiah 1:1); but in the Hebrew and the remaining editions: 'Words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah,' (Jeremiah 1:1 superscription) and all agreed to say: 'Words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah.' Why then 'Words of Jeremiah'? Because his opening toward those not wanting to hear was: Hear my words.

And we also sometimes do such things when it appears profitable to us. Sometimes we bring words to those from the nations wanting to lead them to the faith, and if we see that they are slandered against Christianity and abominate the name and hate to hear that this word is of Christians, we do not pretend to speak a useful word of Christians. But when that word has been built up according to power by us, and we seem to take the hearer as one who has not heard what was said as it chanced, then we confess that this praiseworthy word was a word of Christians. And we do something near to the one who said no longer 'Thus says the Lord' but: Hear words of me, Jeremiah. These things because of 'I became a laugh.' And we are indignant if ever speaking we are laughed at, where such a Jeremiah says: 'I became a laugh all the day.' (Luke 16:14)

before: If then he says, as it were: first I sent Israel away because of the sins, and I sent him into a removal, and Judah, hearing what had happened to Israel, did not turn — he is speaking about our sins.

The things that happened to Israel are read, and the falls concerning that people. We ought to fear: 'if he did not spare the natural branches, how much more not you?' (Romans 11:21–22) If, not sparing those who boast to be a cultivated olive, those rooted into the root of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God who is kind and also a lover of man cut them out, how much more will he not spare us?

For he is not kind and not severe, nor severe and not kind. If he were only kind, and not severe, we would have despised his kindness still more. If he were severe, and not kind, perhaps we would even have despaired over our sins. But now, as God — for we who repent need his kindness, and we who remain in sins need his severity — God is both kind and severe.

And he speaks to us through the prophets and says: 'Have you seen what the dwelling of Israel has done to me?' (Romans 11:24) Understand that Israel as that people. 'She went upon every high mountain and under every shady tree.' (Jeremiah 3:6)

If you see the Pharisee going up into the temple boastfully, not striking his own breast, not caring for his own evils, but saying, 'I thank you that I am not as the rest of men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this tax-collector; I fast twice in the sabbath, I tithe what I have,' (Luke 18:11–12) you will see that he has gone up 'upon every high mountain' in a blameworthy way, and having loved high-mindedness, and according to boast and according to pride every high hill, and has come to be 'under every tree' not fruit-bearing, but 'of a grove.' For a grove-tree is one thing, and a tree planted into groves is another: when they plant trees, they do not plant the fruit-bearing ones, not a fig, not a vine, but only, for pleasure, trees without fruit. You will find the words of the heterodox like that, and the beauties of their persuasions, not turning those who hear.

When then someone gives himself to such words, he has gone 'under every grove-tree.' He did not say 'every tree' and stop, nor again add 'every fruit-bearing tree,' but said 'under every grove-tree.' For this reason you will understand why the lawgiver says: 'You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God, and you shall not make a grove.' (Deuteronomy 16:21) For you have the name of the grove itself forbidden.

And he speaks to us through the prophets and says: 'Have you seen what the dwelling of Israel has done to me?' (Jeremiah 3:6) Understand that Israel as that people. 'She went upon every high mountain and under every shady tree.' (Jeremiah 3:6)

If you see the Pharisee going up into the temple boastfully, not striking his own breast, not caring for his own evils, but saying, 'I thank you that I am not as the rest of men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this tax-collector; I fast twice in the sabbath, I tithe what I have,' (Luke 18:11–12) you will see that he has gone up 'upon every high mountain' in a blameworthy way, and having loved high-mindedness, and according to boast and according to pride every high hill, and has come to be 'under every tree' not fruit-bearing, but 'of a grove.' For a grove-tree is one thing, and a tree planted into groves is another: when they plant trees, they do not plant the fruit-bearing ones, not a fig, not a vine, but only, for pleasure, trees without fruit. You will find the words of the heterodox like that, and the beauties of their persuasions, not turning those who hear.

When then someone gives himself to such words, he has gone 'under every grove-tree.' He did not say 'every tree' and stop, nor again add 'every fruit-bearing tree,' but said 'under every grove-tree.' For this reason you will understand why the lawgiver says: 'You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God, and you shall not make a grove.' (Deuteronomy 16:21) For you have the name of the grove itself forbidden.

before: These things, then, show that the words are not false and that it is Samuel who has come up. What then is a medium doing here? What is a medium doing about the bringing-up of the righteous man’s soul? That first speaker fled—so as not to seem to have a contest against so many other questions in the passage—and says: “It is not Samuel; the demon lies, since the Scripture cannot lie.” (Psalm 16:10) But the Scripture’s words are not from the demon’s person but from her own: “And she saw Samuel,” (Luke 8:43) “Saul said…”—the things spoken from Samuel. How then will the medium’s matters in the passage appear when solved?

I ask the one who said the earlier things (“Samuel in Hades?” and what follows) and let him answer the question: Who is greater, Samuel or Jesus the Christ? Who is greater, the prophets or Jesus the Christ? Who is greater, Abraham or Jesus the Christ? Here no one who has once come to know the Lord as Jesus Christ, the one proclaimed beforehand by the prophets, will dare to say that the Christ is not greater than the prophets.

When therefore you confess that Jesus Christ is greater—Christ in Hades, or did he not come to be there? Is what was said in the Psalms not true, interpreted by the apostles in their Acts, concerning the Savior’s having gone down into Hades? It is written that the fifteenth Psalm is borne upon him: “For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption.” (Acts 2:27–31) Then Jesus Christ is in Hades. Do you fear to say that yes—and there too he goes down to prophesy and to come to the other souls?

Then after this if he answers that Christ has gone down into Hades, I will say: Christ has gone down into Hades to do what—to conquer, or to be conquered by death? And he has come down into those regions not as a slave of those there but as a master wrestling—as we said earlier when interpreting the twenty-second Psalm: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls enclosed me; they opened their mouth at me, like a lion seizing and roaring. My bones were scattered.” (Psalm 22:12–14) We remember, if we remember, the sacred writings; for I remember them said toward the twenty-second Psalm. Therefore the Savior has come down to save; has he come down there proclaimed beforehand by the prophets, or not? But here he was proclaimed beforehand by the prophets, and elsewhere he comes down not through prophets? And Moses proclaims him as about to sojourn with the human race, so that it is well said by our Lord and Savior: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5:46–47) And Christ has sojourned in this life, and Christ is proclaimed beforehand as sojourning in this life. But if Moses prophesies him here, do you not want him to have gone down there also, so that he may prophesy that Christ will come?

What then? Moses—yes—but not the prophets after him? And not Samuel? What is out of place in physicians going down to those who are badly off? Those were many physicians; but my Lord and Savior is chief physician; for even the desire within, which cannot be healed by others, he himself heals—which “could not be healed by anyone” of the physicians; Christ Jesus heals it. Do not fear; do not be stunned: Jesus has come to be in Hades, and the prophets before him, and they proclaim beforehand Christ’s sojourn.

before: 'Why do those who hate me overpower?' (John 18:36) He had many affairs; he suffered from those not wanting to hear what is true, and those were more powerful than him here in this age, since the kingdom of God is not from this age but from the better places, as the Savior says: 'If my kingdom were from this world, my servants would have fought, that I not be handed over to the Jews.' So those grieving the prophet overpowered him in this world. That they are strong—look at the martyrs. The judge sits judging and living luxuriously in the lawcourt; the Christian, in whom Christ is being judged, was filled with bitternesses and has been overpowered by the unjust and is condemned.
