before: But the words of God do not stop at 'to uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Suppose the bad things have been uprooted from me, the worse things pulled down: what good is it to me if, in place of what was uprooted, the better things are not planted? What good is it to me if, in place of these, the things that matter are not built up? That is why the words of God first, of necessity, do the 'uproot and pull down and destroy,' (Jeremiah 1:10) and after that the 'build and plant.' And we have always watched in Scripture that the things which look grim, if I may call them so, are named first, then the things that seem cheerful are said second. 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) He did not say, 'I will make alive,' and after that, 'I will kill.' For it is impossible that what God has made alive should be taken away by him or by anyone else. But 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) Whom will I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor. 'And I will make alive,' (Deuteronomy 32:39) so that he may become 'Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ.' (2 Corinthians 6:16)

If the wretched people from the heresies had understood these things, they would not keep putting them forward to us, saying, Do you see how fierce and inhuman the God of the Law is, when he says, 'I will kill, and I will make alive'? Do you not see in the Scriptures a promise of the resurrection of the dead? Or do you not see the resurrection of the dead already making its beginning in each person? 'We were buried' with Christ 'through baptism' and we were raised with him.

So he begins from the grimmer voices, which are necessary — as 'I will kill' — then, having killed, 'and I will make alive. I will strike, and I will heal.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) 'For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives.' (Hebrews 12:6) First he strikes, and after that he heals. 'For he makes one feel pain and again restores.' (Hebrews 12:6) So also here: 'I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down and to destroy and to build and to plant.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Only, first those bad things must be taken from us. God cannot build on the place of the bad building. 'For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness?' (2 Corinthians 6:14) Vice must be uprooted from the foundations. The building of vice must be consumed from our soul, so that after these things the words of God may build and plant.

I cannot understand what is written in any other way: 'Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.' (Jeremiah 1:9) What do the words do? 'To uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Words uproot 'nations'; words pull down kingdoms — not these worldly ones. Think, in a way worthy of words that pull down, worthy of words that uproot, the things uprooted by words, the things pulled down by words. Is there not, in what is being said right now, a power — if God gives it (according to 'the Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power' (Psalm 68:11)) — a power that uproots, if there is any unbelief, any hypocrisy, any vice, any incontinence? Is there not a power that pulls down, if somewhere an idol-shrine has been built in the heart, so that when that is pulled down a temple of God may be built, and the glory of God may be found in the temple built up, and there may be not a grove but a planting, a garden of God, where the temple of God is, in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power to the ages of the ages. Amen.

before: The one judging the condemned grants place and does not immediately bear the end of punishment upon the transgressor. Therefore, 'judging briefly, he punishes.' This is exemplified in Leviticus, where prior punishments are recorded before subsequent penalties. The Lord says, 'If you do not turn back, I will add seven more plagues.' (Leviticus 26:18) Another punishment is again described: 'If you do not turn back, but go astray, I will go with you in a sideways manner.' (Matthew 23:37–38) You will find God measuring punishments with mercy, as He desires to lead the transgressor to repentance, not wholly destroying them.

Thus, as much as occurred regarding the people through speech, the word threatens them and says they will be convinced after these things. 'In those days, the Lord your God will not strike you to destruction,' (Jeremiah 5:18) if these things especially reach even the future punishments, unless one who has power from things occurring in life regarding the people turns to them. For I would say, as 'they worship heavenly things by example and shadow,' so the people were punished by example and shadow of true punishments for their sins, as all punishment under the law and prophets contains the shadow of true punishments.

Therefore, since their end upon sins did not occur but at a final time, there will never be punishment upon the transgressors after the exodus. The end upon Jerusalem was when the captivity of Nebuchadnezzar occurred. Although someone might say that even then there was no end, nor upon the Maccabees. But the end of the people is upon the presence of my Lord Jesus Christ. For the Savior did not say to them, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' as He did not forgive them. When He wept over Jerusalem, saying, 'Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I desired to gather your children as a bird gathers its brood under its wings, and you would not!' 'Behold, your house is left to you desolate.' The house is left, surrounded by armies of Jerusalem, as the desolation of it has drawn near. Then after their transgression, salvation came to us. They were punished, but the end did not come upon them as the presence of my Lord Jesus.

before: 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations.' (Jeremiah 1:5) If you look for this in Jeremiah — 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5) — watch later on: he is commanded to prophesy 'against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 48:1) and there is a heading, 'What Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 25:13) against Elam, against Damascus, against Moab. And we have it that he 'prophesied against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 25:13) as regards the letter of 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations,' (Jeremiah 1:5) said to him.

If it is a matter of the higher sense: if of Jeremiah, we have already spoken; if of the Savior, what need is there even to say it? He truly prophesied to all the nations. For he is, as he is ten thousand other things, also a prophet. As he is high priest, as he is savior, as he is physician, so he is also prophet. Moses, prophesying about him, did not say only 'a prophet,' but said it with a special force: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your brothers, like me (Deuteronomy 18:15); him you shall hear, and it shall be that whoever does not hear that prophet shall be destroyed from his people.' (Jeremiah 49:23)

This one, then, is also the prophet set 'to the nations,' and he received grace from God poured out on his lips, so that not only when he was present in the body, but also now, when he is present in power and in the Spirit, he may prophesy 'to all the nations,' so that from all the nations his prophecy may reach its end and draw men to salvation (Acts 3:22–23) (Psalm 45:2).

And he has uttered the same voice as David who said: “they seated me in dark places as eternal dead” (Psalm 143:3)—this both through the prisons from the enemies and at once through the calamities from God; for trials are darkness of a soul. before: 'I was sitting alone.' And the words are managed here. Whenever there is a multitude of sinners and they do not bear the righteous living righteously, it is not out of place for one fleeing the council of wickedness to imitate the one who said: 'I was sitting alone,' to imitate also Elijah who says: 'Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my soul to take it.' (1 Kings 19:10, 14) And perhaps even if you examine more deeply 'I was sitting alone,' you will find some mind worthy of prophetic depth. Whenever we imitate the life of the many, so as not to be withdrawn and better and exceptional beside the many, I cannot say: 'I was sitting alone,' but: I was sitting with many.

But when my life becomes hard to imitate, so that I become so great that no one is near me in character, in word, in deeds, in wisdom, then I can say—because of being alone such and no one imitating me—'I was sitting alone.'

So it is possible even if you are not an elder and not a bishop and not honored with some church honor to say this, to zealously imitate 'I was sitting alone' and take up a life so as to say: 'I was sitting alone.' 'Because I was filled with bitternesses.' (Jeremiah 15:17) If 'narrow and afflicted is the way,' how does your feast come to be with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says 'you shall eat unleavened breads upon bitter herbs.' (Exodus 12:8; Num 9:11) What the word wants saying that the one feasting to God must eat 'unleavened breads upon bitter herbs' (Galatians 4:16) must be considered. The apostle interpreted the unleavened breads; the interpretation is not mine; but what follows of the interpretation must necessarily be near the apostolic interpretation.

The apostle interpreted the things about the unleavened breads saying: 'Let us feast not in old leaven nor in leaven of wickedness and evil, but in unleavened breads of sincerity and truth.' (1 Corinthians 5:8) It is necessary to give the account about the bitter herbs following upon the unleavened breads being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you eat with bitter herbs the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth—as Paul. Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.' (2 Corinthians 11:27–28)

So the law said: 'You shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs'; and it did not say: you shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs until you are filled, as upon certain other things it has been said: 'You shall eat and be filled.' But the prophet presses further saying that I did not eat bitterness, but 'I was filled with bitternesses'; as much strength as there was I partook of bitter affairs, so as to partake with the fullest bitter herbs.

Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.' (2 Corinthians 11:27–28)

So the law said: 'You shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs'; and it did not say: you shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs until you are filled, as upon certain other things it has been said: 'You shall eat and be filled.' But the prophet presses further saying that I did not eat bitterness, but 'I was filled with bitternesses'; as much strength as there was I partook of bitter affairs, so as to partake with the fullest bitter herbs.

before: Everyone who has received words from God and has the grace of the heavenly words has received them in order 'to uproot nations and kingdoms and to pull them down.' (Jeremiah 1:10) But if it is said that everyone who has received words from God 'uproots nations and kingdoms,' do not take the nations and the kingdoms for me in a bodily way. Look at human souls, ruled by sin, as the apostle said: 'Do not let sin reign in our mortal body.' (Romans 6:12) And seeing the many kinds of sins, take the nations and the kingdoms as a figure: the bad things in the souls of men, which are uprooted and pulled down by the words of God given either to Jeremiah or to anyone at all.

The first things, which press us as regards the Savior, can also fit Jeremiah; and the second things can fit Jeremiah for the one who knows how to read them as a figure. Someone among the hearers will say to me: Work the other reading too, and try to show that all that is written fits the Savior. Do not be anxious about the second things. It is clear that the Savior uprooted the kingdoms of the devil and pulled down the nations, taking away the life of the nations. Here, at what seems ill-sounding as regards the Savior, work the word somehow: how can the Savior say, 'I do not know how to speak, because I am younger,' (Jeremiah 1:6) and the rest? You see that the argument is in a tight place.

We know the Savior is Lord. We are seeking, according to the dignity of the Word and according to the truth, to refer these things to the Savior. Witnesses must be taken from the Scriptures. For our guesses, if they have no witness, and our interpretations, are not to be trusted. And 'every word shall be established at the mouth of two or three witnesses' (Deuteronomy 19:15) fits interpretations more than it fits men, so that I may establish the words of the interpretation by taking two witnesses from the New and the Old Covenant, taking three from gospel, from prophet, from apostle. For so every word will stand.

How then can we refer these things to the Savior? Bring the Old Covenant as a witness: 'Before the child knows good or evil, he refuses evil to choose the good.' (Isaiah 7:15–16) And these things are said outright about the Savior in Isaiah: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.' (Isaiah 7:14) And there it is added: 'before the child knows.' (Luke 2:40) And if an example must also be taken from the gospel: Jesus, not yet become a man but still a child, since 'he emptied himself,' was advancing. For no one who is already perfected advances; he advances who still needs advance. So he 'advanced in stature, advanced in wisdom, advanced in grace with God and men.' If he emptied himself coming down here, and emptying himself was taking again from what he had emptied himself of, having emptied himself willingly, what is strange if he also advanced 'in wisdom and stature and grace with God and men,' (Luke 2:52) and if what I set down from Isaiah is true of him: before he knows good or evil he will choose the good and refuse evil?

before: We want to understand the words spoken to Jerusalem with much threat, which run like this: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? Or who will look gloomy over you? Or who will turn back to ask after your peace? You have turned away from me, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 15:5)

'You will go backward, and I will stretch out my hand against you and destroy you, and I will no longer spare you. And I will scatter them in dispersion.' (Jeremiah 15:6-7) Then: 'I have been made childless. Helplessness has seized me.' (Lamentations 1:16 (echo)) I take as an example a certain enemy proved against the one who reigns on earth: that it is not permitted even to give him a share of mercy, lest someone seem to strike against the king who condemned him. And it is not permitted even to pity such a one. Some go further and do not even look gloomy over him, lest by looking gloomy they seem displeased at what the king judged. If you have understood this, look with me at the one condemned by God through his many sins, and see such a person—while there are legions of angels appointed to help human nature—pitied by no one.

For each of the angels, seeing that the one who condemned is God, that the one turned away from is the Creator, and that the nature of the sins is such that the good God was compelled—so to speak—to bring the vote against the sinner, each of those who see does not spare, does not look gloomy, does not pity, does not come back so as to plead concerning peace toward such a one.

So let this Jerusalem (for so it will be said according to the letter) have sinned against my Jesus and done such things that Jesus says about her: 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing.' (Matthew 23:37 (watchtower in a cucumber field))

'Look—your house is left to you.' Let this Jerusalem be left as she has been left. Let the angels who always help Jerusalem—through whom Moses' law also was arranged, 'arranged through angels by the hand of a mediator'—leave Jerusalem and say: her sins have become great; they killed Jesus; they laid hands on the Christ.

As long as the sins were still smaller, we could still plead and intercede about them; we could spare Jerusalem. Who will spare for this? 'If a man sinning sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?' 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become a shaking.' And it is said to this one first: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?' We do not look gloomy over Jerusalem and her disasters and what has happened to that whole people—for by their trespass our salvation has come, to provoke them to jealousy.

Since their trespass has become so great a sin that the Lord's voice is spoken—'Who then will spare you'—I too say to the one who killed my Jesus: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?'

before: 'Behold, they say to me: Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come. But I did not grow weary following after you.' (Matthew 16:24) Jesus says to you: 'Take up your cross and follow me,' and 'Leave all things and follow me,' and 'Whoever does not leave father and mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple.' (Matthew 10:37-38) If then you become such that you always follow Jesus, you will also follow, and as long as you follow you will not grow weary; for 'there will be no toil in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel.' (Numbers 23:21) There is no labor for the one following Jesus; the very following takes away the labor.

Therefore he himself says, so that we may no longer grow weary—having grown weary before we began to follow him: 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' (Matthew 11:28) If then, laboring, we come to him and follow him, we will say: 'But I did not grow weary following after you.'

And it is consequent for us to say also: 'I did not desire a human day.' There is a day of a human, and there is a day of God. Let each of us desire the day of the resurrection of the holy ones, not that day concerning which it is written: 'Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; and this is darkness and not light.' Who is the one who says: 'And I did not desire a human day'? The clarity of the word will convict us that we have desired a human day. Often when we have fallen sick and come into a fantasy of death, at the departure we beg the brothers who watch over us and say: Ask for me a leave, ask for me to remain in life. Saying these things we do not desire a holy day of God, but a human day. Therefore putting away love of the body and the desire for a human day, let us seek to see that day in which we will obtain the blessedness in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages. Amen.

before: These things the one who does not want to accept the contest will say—that it is not really Samuel who was brought up. But since one must be fair-minded in hearing the Scriptures, and the argument has plausibly buzzed around us and can truly disturb and move us, let us see whether the Scripture has been understood by the one who does not accept this, or whether he argues from reputable points yet says things contrary to what is written.

For what things are written? “And the woman said, ‘Whom shall I bring up for you?’” (1 Samuel 28:11–14) Whose person is it that says, “the woman said”? Is it the person of the Holy Spirit, from whom the Scripture is believed to have been written, or of someone else? For the narrative person everywhere—as even those practiced in all sorts of discourses know—is the person of the writer; and the writer for these words is believed to be not a human being, but the Holy Spirit who moved human beings as writer. Therefore the Holy Spirit says: “And the woman said, ‘Whom shall I bring up for you?’ And he said, ‘Samuel for me.’ Who says: ‘And the woman saw Samuel, and the woman cried out with a great voice, saying…’?” (1 Samuel 28:15–17)

We will say to that one who has so buzzed against us and said countless things as though Samuel were not in Hades: “The woman saw Samuel”—the narrative voice said this—“and the woman cried out with a great voice and said to Saul, ‘Why have you deceived me? And you are Saul.’ And the king said to her, ‘What is it? Do not fear; what have you seen?’ And the woman said to Saul, ‘I have seen gods coming up from the earth.’ And he said to her, ‘What is their appearance?’ And she said to him, ‘An elderly man coming up, and he himself wrapped in a double cloak, an ephod.’ She says she has seen even the priestly garment.

I know that the one from that argument says: “No wonder; for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. So it is no great thing if his servants also transform themselves as servants of righteousness.” (2 Corinthians 11:14–15) But what is it that “the woman saw”? “Samuel.” And why has it not been said: “The woman saw a demon that pretended to be Samuel”? But it is written that “Saul knew that it is Samuel.” If it were not Samuel, it ought to have been written: “Saul supposed him to be Samuel.” But now it is written: “Saul knew”—and no one knows what is not; therefore “Saul knew that it is Samuel,” “and he fell on his face on the earth and worshiped.”

Then again the person of the Scripture: “And Samuel said to Saul, ‘Why have you provoked me to bring me up?’” “Said,” says the Scripture that must be believed—“Samuel said, ‘Why have you provoked me to bring me up?’” Then Saul answers this: “The foreigners are fighting hard against me, and God has stood away from me and has not answered me any longer, and even by the hand of the prophets and in dreams I have called, that he might show me what I should do.” Again the Scripture has not spoken otherwise, but that Samuel himself said: “And why have you inquired of me? And the Lord has stood away from you.” Does he speak truly or falsely when he says these things: “The Lord has stood away from you and has become against you and has made another for himself, as he spoke by my hand, and he will tear the kingdom from your hand”—and a demon prophesies about Israel’s kingdom? What does the opposing argument say? You see how great a contest there is in the Word of God, needing also hearers able to hear holy words—great and secret words about the departure—while the earlier things are still being questioned and the later are not yet clear.
